1.1 Introduction
In Class IX, you began your exploration of the world of real numbers and encountered
irrational numbers. We continue our discussion on real numbers in this chapter. We
begin with very important properties of positive integers in Sections 1.2, namely the
Euclid’s division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
Euclid’s division algorithm, as the name suggests, has to do with divisibility of
integers. Stated simply, it says any positive integer a can be divided by another positive
integer b in such a way that it leaves a remainder r that is smaller than b. Many of you
probably recognise this as the usual long division process. Although this result is quite
easy to state and understand, it has many applications related to the divisibility proper

integers. You already know that every composite number
can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way—this important fact is the
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Again, while it is a result that is easy to state and
understand, it has some very deep and significant applications in the field of mathematics.
We use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic for two main applications. First, we
use it to prove the irrationality of many of the numbers you studied in Class IX, such as

1.2 The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a
product of its prime factors. For instance, 2 = 2, 4 = 2 × 2, 253 = 11 × 23, and so on.
Now, let us try and look at natural numbers from the other direction. That is, can any
natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers? Let us see.
Take any collection of prime numbers, say 2, 3, 7, 11 and 23. If we multiply
some or all of these numbers, allowing them to repeat as many times as we wish,
we can produce a large collection of positive integers (In fact, infinitely many).
Let us list a few :
7 × 11 × 23 = 1771
3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 5313

23 × 3 × 73 = 8232

and so on.

Theorem 1.1 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) : Every composite
number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation
is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every composite number can
be factorised as a product of primes. Actually it says more. It says that given any
composite number it can be factorised as a product of prime numbers in a ‘unique’
way, except for the order in which the primes occur. That is, given any composite
number there is one and only one w

ch
these primes are written. This fact is also stated in the following form:
The prime factorisation of a natural number is unique, except for the order
of its factors.

Now, that you have studied about all the three measures of central tendency, let
us discuss which measure would be best suited for a particular requirement.
The mean is the most frequently used measure of central tendency because it
takes into account all the observations, and lies between the extremes, i.e., the largest
and the smallest observations of the entire data. It also enables us to compare two or
more distributions. For example, by comparing the average (mean) results of students
of different schools of a particular examination, we can conclude which school has a
better performance.
However, extreme values in the data affect the mean. For example, the mean of
classes having frequencies more or less the same is a good representative of the data.
But, if one class ha

ems where individual observations are not important, and we wish to find
out a ‘typical’ observation, the median is more appropriate, e.g., finding the typical
productivity rate of workers, average wage in a country, etc. These are situations
where extreme values may be there. So, rather than the mean, we take the median as
a better measure of central tendency.
In situations which require establishing the most frequent value or most popular
item, the mode is the best choice, e.g., to find the most popular T.V. programme being
watched, the consumer item in greatest demand, the colour of the vehicle used by
most of the people, etc.

A1.1 Introduction
The ability to reason and think clearly is extremely useful in our daily life. For example,
suppose a politician tells you, ‘If you are interested in a clean government, then you
should vote for me.’ What he actually wants you to believe is that if you do not vote for
him, then you may not get a clean government. Similarly, if an advertisement tells you,
‘The intelligent wear XYZ shoes’, what the company wants you to conclude is that if
you do not wear XYZ shoes, then you are not intelligent enough. You can yourself
observe that both the above statements may mislead the general public. So, if we
understand the process of reasoning correctly, we do not fall into such traps
unknowingly.
The correct use of reasoning is at the core of mathematics, especiall

main tool, we use in constructing a proof, is the process of deductive reasoning.

is. Then, we proceed to sharpen our skills in deductive reasoning using several examples.
We shall also deal with the concept of negation and finding the negation of a given
statement. Then, we discuss what it means to find the converse of a given statement.
Finally, we review the ingredients of a proof learnt in Class IX by analysing the proofs

This introductory page sets the stage for the chapter on Real Numbers, reviewing concepts like irrational numbers from Class IX. It outlines the main topics to be covered: Euclid's Division Algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, both applied to positive integers. The chapter will explore their use in finding HCFs, proving the irrationality of numbers, and understanding the decimal expansions of rational numbers.

This page introduces the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, stating that every natural number can be uniquely expressed as a product of its prime factors. It demonstrates how prime numbers can be multiplied to form composite numbers and then illustrates the reverse process of factorising a composite number into its prime factors using a factor tree.

This page introduces the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, stating that every composite number can be uniquely expressed as a product of prime numbers, irrespective of the order of the factors. It illustrates this with factorization examples and provides historical context, mentioning Euclid's early work and Carl Friedrich Gauss's proof.

This page introduces the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, stating that every composite number can be uniquely expressed as a product of prime numbers in ascending order. It demonstrates how this theorem applies to divisibility checks, such as determining if `4^n` can end with the digit zero. The page then reviews the prime factorisation method for finding the HCF and LCM of two numbers, defining them based on powers of prime factors. Finally, it presents the crucial relationship: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b.

This page focuses on finding the HCF (Highest Common Factor) and LCM (Least Common Multiple) of integers using the prime factorization method. It illustrates the process for both two and three numbers through worked examples. A crucial point highlighted is that the product of two numbers equals the product of their HCF and LCM, a relationship that does not extend to three or more numbers.

This page introduces the concept of irrational numbers and outlines the objective of proving their irrationality, specifically for numbers like √2, √3, √5, and √p. It revisits the definition of an irrational number and provides several examples. The page then presents and proves Theorem 1.2, which states that if a prime number 'p' divides 'a²', then 'p' must also divide 'a', using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Finally, it sets up the proof by contradiction for Theorem 1.3, which asserts that √2 is irrational.

This page demonstrates the proof by contradiction for the irrationality of numbers like √2 and √3. It explains the method of assuming the number is rational, expressing it as a fraction of coprime integers, and then deriving a contradiction that shows the initial assumption must be false. The proofs rely on the property that if a prime number divides a squared integer, it also divides the integer itself (Theorem 1.2).

This page elucidates the method of proof by contradiction to establish the irrationality of numbers. It reiterates fundamental properties concerning operations (sum, difference, product, quotient) between rational and irrational numbers. The text then presents two worked examples, demonstrating how to prove that expressions like 5 - √3 and 3√2 are irrational by showing that an assumption of their rationality leads to a logical contradiction.

This page concludes a discussion on irrational numbers by confirming 3√2 as irrational and presents exercises for proving the irrationality of various expressions involving square roots. It also provides a summary of key chapter concepts, including the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic regarding unique prime factorisation and a divisibility property of primes. Finally, it introduces formulas for calculating the HCF and LCM of three numbers, clarifying that the simple product relationship (HCF * LCM = product of numbers) does not extend to three numbers.

This page introduces the concept of polynomials in one variable and defines the degree of a polynomial as the highest power of the variable. It categorizes polynomials based on their degree: linear (degree 1), quadratic (degree 2), and cubic (degree 3). The general form of a quadratic polynomial is provided, and examples of expressions that are not polynomials are also included.

This page introduces the concept of evaluating a polynomial `p(x)` at a specific real number `k`, resulting in `p(k)`. It then defines a 'zero of a polynomial' as any real number `k` for which `p(k) = 0`. Examples demonstrate finding zeroes for quadratic polynomials and derive the general formula for finding the zero of a linear polynomial `ax + b` as `k = -b/a`, highlighting the relationship between zeroes and coefficients. The page concludes by setting up the discussion on the geometrical meaning of polynomial zeroes.

This page establishes the geometrical interpretation of the zero of a linear polynomial. It demonstrates that the zero of a linear polynomial `ax + b` is the x-coordinate where its graph, the straight line `y = ax + b`, intersects the x-axis. Using `y = 2x + 3` as an example, it illustrates how the x-intercept `(-3/2, 0)` corresponds to the polynomial's zero, `-3/2`. The page concludes by introducing the concept of the geometrical meaning of zeros for quadratic polynomials.

This page introduces the graphical representation of quadratic polynomials, showing their graphs are parabolas. It establishes that the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial correspond to the x-coordinates where its parabolic graph intersects the x-axis. The direction in which the parabola opens (upwards or downwards) is determined by the sign of the coefficient 'a' in the general form `y = ax² + bx + c`.

This page explains the graphical interpretation of the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial of the form `ax^2 + bx + c`. It illustrates two main cases: when the graph (a parabola) intersects the x-axis at two distinct points, indicating two distinct zeroes, and when the graph touches the x-axis at exactly one point, indicating one unique zero (or two coincident zeroes). The x-coordinates of these intersection points represent the zeroes of the polynomial.

This page concludes the discussion on the geometrical meaning of zeroes for quadratic polynomials by illustrating cases where a quadratic polynomial has no real zeroes. It emphasizes that a quadratic polynomial can have at most two zeroes. The page then transitions to exploring the geometrical meaning of zeroes for cubic polynomials, specifically introducing y = x³ - 4x and providing a table of values to prepare for graphing it.

This page establishes the fundamental relationship between the zeroes of a polynomial and the x-coordinates where its graph intersects the x-axis. It uses the cubic polynomial `y = x³ - 4x` to illustrate how its three zeroes correspond to three x-intercepts. Further examples with `y = x³` and `y = x³ - x²` demonstrate varied behaviors of cubic polynomial graphs and their zeroes.

This page explains the geometrical meaning of the zeroes of a polynomial, which are the x-coordinates where the graph intersects the x-axis. It establishes that a polynomial of degree 'n' can have at most 'n' zeroes, elaborating on examples of cubic polynomials. A worked example demonstrates how to visually determine the number of zeroes for various polynomial graphs by counting their intersections with the x-axis.

This page introduces the concept of finding the number of zeroes of a polynomial by interpreting its graph's x-intercepts, providing six visual examples for practice. It then transitions to exploring the algebraic relationship between the zeroes and coefficients of a quadratic polynomial, illustrating how to find zeroes through factorization by splitting the middle term.

This page introduces the fundamental relationship between the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial and its coefficients. It uses two numerical examples to illustrate that the sum of the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial `ax^2 + bx + c` is `-b/a` and the product of the zeroes is `c/a`. The page then provides a general algebraic derivation to prove these relationships.

This page introduces the fundamental relationship between the zeroes and coefficients of a quadratic polynomial, presenting formulas for the sum and product of zeroes. It then illustrates these relationships through two detailed worked examples. These examples demonstrate how to find the zeroes of quadratic polynomials by factoring and subsequently verify the derived coefficient formulas.

This page explains the relationship between the zeroes and coefficients of quadratic and cubic polynomials. For quadratic polynomials, it defines how the sum and product of zeroes relate to the coefficients. It then extends this concept to cubic polynomials, demonstrating how the sum of zeroes, the product of zeroes, and the sum of products of zeroes taken two at a time, relate to their respective coefficients.

This page defines the relationships between the zeroes (α, β, γ) and coefficients (a, b, c, d) of a cubic polynomial (ax³ + bx² + cx + d). It presents formulas for the sum of zeroes, the sum of products of zeroes taken two at a time, and the product of all zeroes. A worked example demonstrates how to verify given values as zeroes of a cubic polynomial and subsequently confirm these relationships using the derived formulas.

This page summarizes key concepts about polynomials, including their classification by degree (linear, quadratic, cubic) and the graphical interpretation of their zeroes. It also details the maximum number of zeroes for quadratic and cubic polynomials. Crucially, it provides the fundamental relationships between the zeroes and coefficients for both quadratic and cubic polynomials.

This page introduces the concept of 'Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables' by presenting a real-world scenario. It uses a word problem about a girl named Akhila at a fair, where she spends money on rides and a game, to illustrate situations that can be represented and solved using linear equations in two variables. The text prompts the reader to consider how they might solve such a problem, hinting at the mathematical tools to be covered.

This page introduces the graphical method for solving pairs of linear equations in two variables. It defines key terms like 'consistent,' 'inconsistent,' and 'dependent' pairs of equations based on whether they have one, no, or infinitely many solutions, respectively. The page also summarizes the geometric interpretations of these solutions, explaining that lines can intersect, be parallel, or coincide.

This page explains how to classify a pair of linear equations in two variables based on the ratios of their coefficients. It shows how these ratios directly correspond to the graphical representation (intersecting, coincident, or parallel lines) and the algebraic interpretation (unique solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solution). An example is introduced to illustrate checking consistency and solving graphically.

This page demonstrates the graphical method for solving a pair of linear equations in two variables, illustrating how a common point (intersection) on lines represents a unique solution for a consistent system. It provides an example to graphically identify if a pair of equations has no solution, a unique solution, or infinitely many solutions by examining their algebraic forms and graphical properties. The page concludes with a word problem requiring the formulation of linear equations from a real-world scenario.

This page illustrates the graphical method for solving a system of linear equations in two variables. It uses a worked example to demonstrate how to formulate equations from a word problem, create tables of coordinate pairs, plot the lines, and identify their intersection point as the solution. An exercise is provided to allow students to practice applying this method to similar real-world problems.

This page focuses on the analysis and application of pairs of linear equations in two variables. Students learn to classify systems of equations as intersecting, parallel, or coincident, and as consistent or inconsistent, by comparing the ratios of their coefficients. The page also includes exercises requiring students to solve word problems, generate equations based on desired graphical outcomes, and solve systems graphically to find geometric properties like triangle vertices.

This page introduces algebraic methods for solving pairs of linear equations, emphasizing their advantages over graphical methods for non-integral solutions. It specifically details the 'Substitution Method' as an algebraic technique. A worked example demonstrates the step-by-step process of solving a system of two linear equations using this method to find the values of both variables.

This page details the step-by-step procedure of the substitution method for solving a pair of linear equations in two variables. It explains how to isolate one variable, substitute its expression into the other equation, and then solve for both variables. A worked example demonstrates applying this method to an age-related word problem, showing the algebraic formulation and solution.

This page demonstrates how to solve systems of linear equations using the substitution method, specifically focusing on cases where there are infinitely many solutions or no solution. It explains the implications of obtaining an identity (e.g., 18=18) or a contradiction (e.g., 8=12) during the solution process, relating them to the geometric interpretation of coinciding or parallel lines, respectively. Word problems are used to illustrate these concepts.

This page introduces Exercise 3.2, which focuses on solving pairs of linear equations in two variables using the substitution method. It includes various problems ranging from direct application of the method to equations with different coefficients (integers, fractions, decimals, irrational numbers) to comprehensive word problems requiring students to form equations first and then solve them. The page also briefly illustrates an inconsistent system of equations leading to a false statement, implying no common solution.

This page introduces the elimination method for solving systems of linear equations in two variables, presenting it as an alternative and often more convenient method than substitution. A detailed worked example illustrates the step-by-step process, which includes scaling equations to make coefficients of one variable equal, subtracting the equations to eliminate that variable, and then substituting the found value back into an original equation to solve for the second variable. The page concludes with a brief remark defining the method.

This page outlines the step-by-step procedure for solving pairs of linear equations using the elimination method. It details how to manipulate equations to eliminate one variable and then solve for the other. The page also explains how to identify cases where a system has infinitely many solutions or no solution, with a worked example illustrating the 'no solution' scenario.

This page illustrates how to solve problems involving two-digit numbers by representing them algebraically and forming a system of linear equations. It demonstrates the use of the elimination method to solve such systems, considering different cases for digit relationships. The page then introduces Exercise 3.3, which includes practice problems for solving linear equations using both elimination and substitution methods, as well as formulating and solving linear equations from various word problems.

This page summarizes key concepts and methods for solving pairs of linear equations in two variables. It covers graphical methods (intersecting, coincident, and parallel lines) and algebraic methods (substitution and elimination). Additionally, it details how the ratios of coefficients (a1/a2, b1/b2, c1/c2) determine whether a system has a unique solution (consistent), no solution (inconsistent), or infinitely many solutions (dependent and consistent).

This page introduces quadratic equations by defining them as quadratic polynomials equated to zero, highlighting their relevance in real-life scenarios. It provides a detailed example of how a practical problem (calculating hall dimensions) can be modeled and solved using a quadratic equation. The text also offers a brief historical perspective on the development and solutions of quadratic equations by ancient civilizations and mathematicians.

This page introduces quadratic equations, beginning with historical context about their discovery and early study. It defines a quadratic equation as an equation of the form `ax^2 + bx + c = 0` where `a, b, c` are real numbers and `a ≠ 0`, clarifying that it is a polynomial of degree 2. The chapter aims to cover finding roots and real-life applications, presenting initial examples of how word problems can be translated into quadratic equations.

This page demonstrates how to form quadratic equations from real-world word problems by translating the given conditions into algebraic expressions. It provides two detailed examples of this process. Additionally, it introduces an example on how to check if a given algebraic equation is a quadratic equation by simplifying it to the standard form `ax² + bx + c = 0`.

This page focuses on how to identify whether a given algebraic equation is a quadratic equation. It demonstrates the necessity of simplifying equations to their standard form, `ax^2 + bx + c = 0`, before determining their degree. Examples show that an equation's initial appearance, whether linear or cubic, can be misleading, and simplification is crucial for correct classification.

This page introduces the concept of roots of a quadratic equation and their equivalence to the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial. It demonstrates the method of finding these roots by factorizing the quadratic polynomial through splitting the middle term. An example is provided to illustrate this factorization method for a specific quadratic equation.

This page explains the method of factorisation to find the roots of quadratic equations. It presents two detailed examples: one for a standard quadratic and another with irrational coefficients. The examples demonstrate how to break down quadratic expressions into linear factors and then solve for x by equating each factor to zero, including cases of repeated roots.

This page illustrates the factorization method for solving quadratic equations through a practical word problem, finding the dimensions of a prayer hall. It then provides a set of practice exercises, including direct quadratic equation solving and various word problems that require forming and solving quadratic equations. The page also introduces the 'Nature of Roots' and presents the quadratic formula, specifically explaining the case where the discriminant `b^2 - 4ac > 0` results in two distinct real roots.

This page introduces the concept of the discriminant ($b^2 - 4ac$) for a quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$. It explains how the sign of the discriminant determines the nature of the roots: positive for two distinct real roots, zero for two equal real roots, and negative for no real roots. The page provides a worked example demonstrating how to calculate the discriminant and determine the nature of roots, and sets up a geometric word problem that will likely lead to a quadratic equation.

This page demonstrates how to apply quadratic equations to solve real-world problems involving geometric constraints. It covers using the discriminant to determine if real solutions exist and then applying the quadratic formula to find these solutions. The importance of interpreting solutions in context, such as ignoring negative distances, is also highlighted. A second example further illustrates finding the discriminant and roots for a quadratic equation that yields equal real roots.

This page summarizes key concepts of quadratic equations, defining their standard form and the relationship between roots and polynomial zeroes. It presents the quadratic formula for finding roots and explains how the discriminant determines the nature of these roots (distinct real, equal real, or no real roots). The page also includes an exercise set applying these concepts to various problems, including word problems.

This page is mostly blank, featuring only a prominent 'NOTE' heading and copyright information. It does not contain any teaching content or pedagogical material related to mathematics. It appears to be a placeholder or a dedicated section for future notes.

This introductory page to "Arithmetic Progressions" highlights how patterns exist in nature and everyday life. It illustrates this with three scenarios: a salary with annual increments, ladder rungs with uniformly decreasing lengths, and a savings scheme with periodic growth. These examples demonstrate various numerical sequences, setting the stage for understanding arithmetic progressions.

This page introduces different types of sequences through practical examples. It demonstrates how sequences can arise from geometric patterns (squares), arithmetic progressions (money accumulation), and biological growth patterns (rabbit reproduction, leading to the Fibonacci sequence). The examples visually and numerically illustrate the formation of these sequences.

This page introduces Arithmetic Progressions (AP) by examining various number patterns. It defines an AP as a list of numbers where each term, after the first, is derived by adding a constant value to the preceding term. This constant value is termed the common difference, and it can be positive, negative, or zero.

This page introduces the concept of an Arithmetic Progression (AP), defining its first term (a), common difference (d), and nth term (an). It provides a formula for the common difference and the general form of an AP. The text also distinguishes between finite and infinite APs and highlights that both the first term and common difference are necessary to define an AP.

This page explains how to determine if a given sequence of numbers is an Arithmetic Progression (AP) by checking if the difference between any two consecutive terms is constant. It defines the first term 'a' and the common difference 'd' and shows how to calculate 'd' using the formula `d = a_{k+1} - a_k`. Several examples are provided to illustrate both the identification of an AP and the calculation of its first term and common difference, along with a counter-example of a sequence that is not an AP.

This page explains how to determine the common difference ('d') in an Arithmetic Progression (AP) by subtracting any term from its succeeding term. It emphasizes correctly calculating 'd' even if the succeeding term is smaller. The page provides examples demonstrating how to find the first term and common difference for a given AP, and how to verify if a list of numbers forms an AP by checking for a constant common difference, then extending the series.

This page focuses on exercises related to Arithmetic Progressions (AP). It presents problems that require students to determine if various real-world situations form an AP, calculate terms of an AP given the first term and common difference, and identify the first term and common difference from a given AP. Additionally, students are asked to identify if a given sequence is an AP and, if so, to find its common difference and extend it.

This page introduces the concept of the nth term of an Arithmetic Progression (AP) through a real-world problem involving a person's monthly salary with annual increments. It demonstrates the calculation of salary for the second, third, fourth, and fifth years, illustrating how a constant increment leads to an AP. The derived pattern lays the groundwork for understanding the general formula for the nth term of an AP.

This page introduces the concept of Arithmetic Progressions (AP) using a practical example of a salary increment. It demonstrates how to calculate a specific term (e.g., 15th or 25th year's salary) by recognizing a pattern of constant addition. Finally, it generalizes this pattern to derive the formula for the nth term of an AP: `a_n = a + (n - 1)d`, where `a` is the first term and `d` is the common difference.

This page introduces the concept of the 'general term' ($a_n$) and 'last term' ($a_m$ or $l$) of an Arithmetic Progression (AP). It demonstrates how to use the formula for the general term to calculate a specific term, find the position of a given term, and determine an entire AP from its individual terms, often involving solving linear equations.

This page demonstrates how to apply the formula for the nth term of an Arithmetic Progression (AP) through several examples. It covers checking if a specific number belongs to a given AP, determining the count of numbers satisfying certain divisibility rules within a range using AP properties, and initiating the process of finding a term from the end of an AP. The importance of the term index 'n' being a positive integer is also highlighted.

This page demonstrates two methods for finding a specific term from the end of an Arithmetic Progression (AP): by calculating the total number of terms and converting the 'from last' position to a 'from start' position, or by reversing the entire AP and finding the term directly. It also illustrates a practical application of APs by showing how accumulated simple interest over successive years forms an arithmetic progression.

This page continues a discussion on Arithmetic Progressions (AP), demonstrating their application in practical scenarios. It first shows how to calculate the 30th term of an AP to find interest over 30 years. Subsequently, Example 10 illustrates how to determine the number of terms (rows) in an AP given the first term, common difference, and the last term, using the nth term formula. The page concludes with Exercise 5.2, which requires students to fill in missing values in a table related to APs.

This page provides a comprehensive set of practice exercises on Arithmetic Progressions (APs). Students are required to calculate specific terms, find missing terms, determine the number of terms, identify which term corresponds to a given value, and solve problems involving relationships between terms of one or more APs. The problems range from direct calculations to multi-step reasoning.

This page includes practice exercises on Arithmetic Progressions (APs) involving finding terms and applying AP concepts to real-world scenarios. It then introduces the concept of finding the 'Sum of First n Terms of an AP' by presenting a motivating word problem. The page further illustrates a historical method for summing an arithmetic series, specifically Gauss's technique for summing integers from 1 to 100, as a precursor to the general formula.

This page derives the formula for the sum of the first 'n' terms of an Arithmetic Progression (AP). It presents the sum in forward and reverse order, adds them term-wise, and simplifies to arrive at the main formula: S = (n/2)[2a + (n-1)d]. Additionally, it introduces alternative forms of the sum formula using the last term, expressed as `S = (n/2)(a + a_n)` or `S = (n/2)(a + l)`.

This page introduces and demonstrates the formula for the sum of the first 'n' terms of an Arithmetic Progression (AP). It provides worked examples showing how to calculate the sum when the first term, common difference, and number of terms are known. A key remark also defines the nth term of an AP as the difference between the sum of 'n' terms and the sum of '(n-1)' terms.

This page demonstrates how to find the number of terms (n) in an Arithmetic Progression (AP) when the first term, common difference, and sum of terms are given, which often leads to solving a quadratic equation. It clarifies why multiple valid solutions for 'n' can occur, specifically when additional terms sum to zero. The page also illustrates how to calculate the sum of the first 'n' positive integers using the AP sum formula.

This page introduces the formula for the sum of the first 'n' positive integers. It then demonstrates how to calculate the sum of terms in an arithmetic progression (AP) given its nth term. The page also includes a word problem to illustrate the application of AP concepts, such as finding specific terms and sums, in real-world scenarios like uniform production increase.

This page continues a worked example demonstrating the application of Arithmetic Progressions (AP) to a real-world production problem. It shows how to solve a system of linear equations to find the first term and common difference, calculate a specific term (10th year's production), and find the sum of a certain number of terms (total production in 7 years). The page concludes with a comprehensive exercise section covering various types of AP problems, including finding sums, specific terms, and unknown parameters.

This page presents a comprehensive set of exercises on Arithmetic Progressions (AP). The problems require students to apply formulas for the nth term and the sum of n terms of an AP to find unknown values such as the number of terms, common difference, specific terms, or sums. Several exercises involve real-world applications of APs, covering scenarios like penalty calculations, prize distribution, tree planting, and measuring spiral lengths.

This page features two word problems and a figure hint, all designed to apply the concepts of arithmetic progressions. The problems involve calculating the number of rows and logs in a stack, and the total distance covered in a potato race, requiring the sum and terms of an arithmetic progression. The hint for a spiral figure suggests another application of arithmetic progressions to geometric shapes.

This page features an optional exercise set (Exercise 5.4) comprising five challenging problems focused on Arithmetic Progressions (APs). The problems test various applications of APs, including finding negative terms, sums of terms, and practical scenarios like ladder construction, house numbering puzzles, and calculating concrete volume for a stepped terrace.

This page provides a summary of Arithmetic Progressions (AP), defining an AP by its fixed common difference and presenting its general form. It outlines formulas for calculating the nth term and the sum of the first n terms, including a version that uses the last term. The page also introduces the concept and formula for the arithmetic mean between two numbers.

This page introduces the concept of similar figures, distinguishing them from congruent figures by emphasizing that similar figures have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. It announces that the chapter will focus on the similarity of triangles and its application, including a proof of Pythagoras Theorem. The introduction also hints at real-world applications of similarity, such as measuring heights of mountains and distances to celestial bodies.

This page introduces the concept of similar figures in geometry, distinguishing it from congruent figures. It explains that similar figures share the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Examples of similar figures include all circles, all squares, and all equilateral triangles, while also highlighting that congruent figures are a subset of similar figures. The page briefly mentions the application of similarity in indirect measurements.

This page introduces the concept of similar figures in geometry, distinguishing it from figures of the same size. It uses real-world examples of photographs, including different sized images of the Taj Mahal and images of a person at different ages, to build an intuitive understanding of similarity. The page culminates in providing a formal definition for the similarity of two polygons, stating that their corresponding angles must be equal and their corresponding sides must be in the same ratio.

This page introduces the concept of similar polygons, using an activity where a quadrilateral's shadow creates an enlarged, similar figure. It explains that two polygons are similar if their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (scale factor or representative fraction). The page emphasizes that similar figures have the same shape but can differ in size.

This page introduces the concept of similar polygons, specifically quadrilaterals, by demonstrating examples where figures are similar (Fig. 6.5). It explains that for polygons to be similar, both their corresponding angles must be equal and their corresponding sides must be in the same ratio. The page also highlights common misconceptions by presenting cases where only one of these conditions is met, showing that the polygons are not similar (Fig. 6.6 and described Fig. 6.7).

This page introduces the concept of similarity in polygons, particularly focusing on quadrilaterals. It clarifies that for two polygons to be similar, both their corresponding angles must be equal AND their corresponding sides must be proportional; satisfying only one condition is not sufficient. The page includes an exercise that tests understanding of these conditions, requiring students to fill in blanks, provide examples, and determine the similarity of given figures.

This page introduces the concept of similarity of triangles, defining conditions such as equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. It highlights that triangles with equal corresponding angles are known as equiangular triangles, and for such triangles, the ratio of any two corresponding sides is always the same, a truth attributed to Thales. The page then presents an activity designed to lead students to empirically discover the Basic Proportionality Theorem (also known as Thales Theorem) by observing segment ratios in a geometric construction.

This page introduces Theorem 6.1, also known as the Basic Proportionality Theorem, which states that a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio. It provides the initial steps of the proof using the concept of the area of a triangle, construction of perpendiculars, and ratios of areas.

This page introduces the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT) through an activity. Students are guided to draw an angle and mark equally spaced points on its arms, then observe that lines connecting points on opposite arms, which divide the sides proportionally, are parallel to each other. This activity demonstrates that if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then the line is parallel to the third side, thus establishing the Converse of BPT.

This page introduces Theorem 6.2, the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem, which states that if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side. It also presents a detailed worked example (Example 1) demonstrating how to derive new proportional relationships between segments and whole sides of a triangle, given that a line is parallel to one of its sides, by applying Theorem 6.1 (Basic Proportionality Theorem) and algebraic manipulation.

This page demonstrates the application of theorems related to parallel lines and proportionality in geometric figures. It provides two worked examples: one showing how to prove a proportionality in a trapezium using the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT), and another using the converse of BPT and properties of corresponding angles to prove a triangle is isosceles.

This page concludes a previous discussion by reiterating the property that sides opposite equal angles in a triangle are equal, thus defining an isosceles triangle. The main content is EXERCISE 6.2, which comprises four problems testing the application of the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT) and its converse in various geometric configurations involving parallel lines within triangles and quadrilaterals.

This page focuses on properties of triangles and quadrilaterals, featuring practice exercises that require applying theorems related to parallel lines and mid-points within triangles, as well as properties of trapeziums. It then introduces the formal criteria for similarity of triangles, defining that two triangles are similar if their corresponding angles are equal and their corresponding sides are in the same proportion.

This page introduces the concept of similar triangles, explaining its symbolic representation and the importance of correct vertex correspondence, distinguishing it from congruence. It highlights that similarity, like congruence, can be established using fewer than all six pairs of corresponding parts. The page then sets up an activity to explore criteria for triangle similarity.

This page introduces the Angle-Angle-Angle (AAA) similarity criterion for triangles, stating that if corresponding angles of two triangles are equal, their corresponding sides are proportional, making the triangles similar. It begins with an activity demonstrating this proportionality and then provides a detailed proof for Theorem 6.3, which formally establishes the AAA criterion.

This page introduces the AA (Angle-Angle) and SSS (Side-Side-Side) similarity criteria for triangles. It states the AA criterion and then uses an activity to demonstrate the SSS criterion, showing that if the sides of two triangles are proportional, their corresponding angles are equal, making the triangles similar. The page clarifies that the SSS criterion is the converse to the idea that proportional sides follow from equal angles.

This page builds upon the concept of triangle similarity by demonstrating how properties of constructed similar triangles lead to the conclusion that if corresponding angles are equal, then corresponding sides are proportional, and vice versa. It clarifies that for triangles, unlike general polygons, only one of these conditions (equal angles or proportional sides) needs to be checked to prove similarity. The page also prepares the reader for an activity to explore the SAS similarity criterion by recalling congruence criteria.

This page introduces the SAS (Side-Angle-Side) similarity criterion for triangles. It demonstrates that if one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of another triangle, and the sides including these angles are proportional, then the two triangles are similar. The page provides an observational example and outlines the setup for a formal proof of this theorem.

This page illustrates the application of similarity criteria for triangles, particularly the AAA (Angle-Angle-Angle) criterion. It provides two worked examples: one demonstrating how to prove triangle similarity using parallel lines and angle properties, and another that sets up a problem to find an unknown angle in a triangle by analyzing given figures and implicitly applying similarity concepts.

This page demonstrates the criteria for similar triangles, including SSS (Side-Side-Side) and SAS (Side-Angle-Side) similarity, along with the property that corresponding angles of similar triangles are equal. It provides two worked examples: one proving triangle similarity and finding angles using algebraic manipulation of side ratios and vertical angles, and another setting up a real-world problem involving a lamp-post, a girl, and her shadow to be solved using similar triangles.

This page illustrates the application of triangle similarity, specifically the AA similarity criterion, to solve both real-world problems and geometric proofs. It demonstrates how to calculate unknown lengths using similar triangles formed by a lamp-post and a person, and how to prove the similarity of smaller triangles and proportionality of medians within larger similar triangles. The properties of proportional sides and equal angles in similar triangles are central to the examples provided.

This page continues a geometrical proof demonstrating triangle similarity. It shows how to prove two triangles are similar using the SAS (Side-Angle-Side) similarity criterion and then further extends the proof to show similarity using the SSS (Side-Side-Side) criterion by establishing proportional sides. The page concludes with an exercise asking students to identify similar triangles and their similarity criteria.

This page primarily focuses on the concept of similar triangles, illustrating various cases with side lengths and angles. It includes two exercises: one requiring the calculation of angles based on similar triangles in a diagram, and another proving a proportionality of sides in a trapezium using similarity criteria.

This page provides a set of challenging exercises focused on proving the similarity of triangles in various geometric configurations. Students are required to apply different similarity criteria (AA, SAS) and properties derived from congruent figures or specific geometric properties like altitudes, angle bisectors, and parallelograms. The problems also involve demonstrating proportional relationships between the sides of similar triangles.

This page provides a summary of key concepts related to similar figures and triangles, including definitions, conditions for polygon similarity, and important triangle similarity criteria like AAA and AA. It also revisits the Basic Proportionality Theorem and its converse. The page concludes with a set of practice exercises that apply these geometric principles to various triangle scenarios and real-world problems.

This page defines three similarity criteria for triangles: SSS (Side-Side-Side), SAS (Side-Angle-Side), and RHS (Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side). The SSS criterion states that if corresponding sides are in the same ratio, angles are equal and triangles are similar. The SAS criterion applies when one angle is equal and the sides including these angles are proportional. The RHS criterion is specifically for right triangles where the hypotenuse and one side are proportional.

This page serves as an introduction to Coordinate Geometry, reviewing foundational concepts like coordinate axes, abscissa, and ordinate from Class IX. It highlights the graphical representation of linear equations as straight lines and quadratic equations as parabolas. The chapter will further delve into calculating the distance between two points and applying the section formula to find coordinates that divide a line segment in a given ratio.

This page introduces the concept of finding the distance between two points, starting with a real-world scenario solvable by the Pythagorean theorem. It then demonstrates how to calculate distances between points lying on the x-axis and y-axis using simple subtraction of coordinates. Finally, it sets the stage for finding the distance between two general points not on the coordinate axes, again hinting at the use of the Pythagorean theorem.

This page demonstrates how to calculate the distance between two points in a Cartesian coordinate system using the Pythagoras theorem. It covers scenarios where points are in the same quadrant and points are in different quadrants, illustrating the necessary geometric constructions to form a right-angled triangle. Specific calculations are provided for two different pairs of points.

This page introduces and derives the distance formula between two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) in a Cartesian coordinate system using the Pythagorean theorem. It highlights the non-negative nature of distance and presents a special case for the distance from the origin. A worked example demonstrates how to apply the formula to determine if three given points form a triangle.

This page focuses on applying coordinate geometry concepts, primarily the distance formula and the converse of the Pythagoras theorem, to determine properties of geometric figures. It provides examples of how to verify if given points form a square by checking side lengths and diagonals, and how to determine if three points are collinear in a real-world context.

This page demonstrates the application of the distance formula to determine if three points are collinear. It then illustrates how to find the algebraic relation between coordinates of a point that is equidistant from two given points, which results in a linear equation. The geometric interpretation of this linear equation as the perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting the two points is also highlighted.

This page is dedicated to 'EXERCISE 7.1' from the Coordinate Geometry chapter, offering a variety of problems to practice the distance formula. It includes questions on finding distances between points, determining collinearity, identifying types of triangles and quadrilaterals, finding points equidistant from others, and solving for unknown coordinates. A worked example demonstrating the application of the distance formula for equidistant points is also provided.

This page introduces the concept of the Section Formula through a practical problem involving positioning a relay tower. It demonstrates how to find the coordinates of a point that divides a line segment in a given ratio using similar triangles and coordinate geometry. The page concludes by setting up the general case for deriving the section formula.

This page details the derivation of the section formula, which calculates the coordinates of a point dividing a line segment in a given ratio. It uses similar triangles and perpendiculars to the x-axis to establish the relationships. The page also presents special cases of the section formula, specifically for a ratio of k:1 and for finding the coordinates of a midpoint.

This page demonstrates the application of the section formula in coordinate geometry. It provides worked examples for two common scenarios: finding the coordinates of a point that divides a line segment in a given ratio internally, and determining the ratio in which a point divides a given line segment.

This page demonstrates the application of the section formula in coordinate geometry. It shows how to determine the ratio in which a given point divides a line segment, using the k:1 method. Furthermore, it illustrates how to find the coordinates of points that trisect a line segment by applying the section formula for different ratios.

This page focuses on applying coordinate geometry formulas to solve problems. It demonstrates how to use the section formula to find the ratio in which the y-axis divides a line segment and determine the coordinates of the intersection point. Additionally, it illustrates the use of the midpoint formula and properties of parallelograms (diagonals bisect each other) to find unknown coordinates of vertices.

This page contains Exercise 7.2, a set of 10 problems designed to reinforce concepts in Coordinate Geometry. The exercises cover topics such as finding coordinates of points dividing a line segment in a given ratio, calculating distances between points, determining ratios of division, and applying coordinate geometry to solve problems involving parallelograms, circles, and rhombuses.

This page summarizes key concepts and formulas from coordinate geometry. It covers the distance formula between two points, the distance of a point from the origin, the section formula for internal division of a line segment, and the midpoint formula. Additionally, it briefly introduces the concept of external division as a topic for higher classes.

This page introduces the concept of trigonometry by highlighting its relevance in solving real-world problems that involve finding unknown lengths or heights using right triangles. It presents two scenarios – finding the height of a minar and the width of a river – to illustrate how trigonometry can be applied to indirect measurement.

This page introduces trigonometry as the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle, highlighting its historical and modern applications in finding distances and heights. It defines 'trigonometric ratios' for acute angles in right triangles and introduces key terminology such as 'opposite side', 'adjacent side', and 'hypotenuse' relative to a specific acute angle. The chapter sets the stage for calculating these ratios and establishing trigonometric identities.

This page introduces the fundamental trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, tangent, cosecant, secant, cotangent) for an acute angle in a right-angled triangle. It defines each ratio using the lengths of the sides relative to the angle (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) and establishes the reciprocal relationships between them. Additionally, it presents the quotient identities for tangent and cotangent, emphasizing the relationship between angles and side lengths.

This page traces the historical evolution of trigonometric terms like 'sine', 'cosine', and 'tangent', highlighting key figures and linguistic origins. It clarifies the proper interpretation of trigonometric notation, stressing that 'sin A' represents the sine of angle A, not a product. The page then introduces a geometric problem involving similar right-angled triangles to set up the concept that trigonometric ratios for a given angle are consistent regardless of the triangle's size, leading to the proportionality of their corresponding sides.

This page explains that the trigonometric ratios of an angle remain constant regardless of the size of the right-angled triangle, provided the angle stays the same. It introduces shorthand notation for powers of trigonometric ratios (e.g., sin²A) and clarifies the distinct meanings of cosec A and sin⁻¹ A. The page concludes with a worked example demonstrating how to determine other trigonometric ratios using the Pythagorean theorem when one ratio is known.

This page introduces trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles, starting with a remark that sine and cosine values are always less than or equal to 1. It then provides a worked example demonstrating how to calculate all six trigonometric ratios for an angle given one ratio, utilizing the Pythagorean theorem. A second example is initiated to prove that if the sines of two acute angles are equal, then the angles themselves are equal, setting up the problem with two right triangles.

This page introduces the concept of trigonometric ratios by demonstrating the similarity of right-angled triangles and showing that ratios of corresponding sides are constant. It then provides a detailed example (Example 3) to calculate the sides of a right-angled triangle using the Pythagorean theorem and determine the values of trigonometric identities like `cos^2 θ + sin^2 θ` and `cos^2 θ - sin^2 θ`.

This page demonstrates the application of trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles through two worked examples. Example 4 verifies a trigonometric identity using the given value of tan A, while Example 5 involves determining sine and cosine values for an angle by first calculating unknown side lengths using the Pythagorean theorem and an algebraic relationship.

This page presents Exercise 8.1, a set of 11 problems focused on practicing the fundamental trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles. Students are required to calculate various ratios given side lengths or one ratio, evaluate trigonometric expressions, verify identities, and critically assess true/false statements about trigonometric functions and notation. The page concludes by introducing the next section on trigonometric ratios for specific angles.

This page details the derivation of trigonometric ratios for a 45-degree angle using a right-angled isosceles triangle. It defines sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec, and cot for 45 degrees with their respective values. Furthermore, it introduces the geometric construction involving an equilateral triangle and its altitude as a precursor to deriving trigonometric ratios for 30 and 60 degrees.

This page details the derivation of trigonometric ratios for special angles 30° and 60° by utilizing an equilateral triangle and its properties. It provides step-by-step calculations for sine, cosine, tangent, and their reciprocals for these angles. Furthermore, it introduces the conceptual understanding of trigonometric ratios for 0° and 90° by illustrating how the sides of a right-angled triangle change as an angle approaches zero.

This page defines the trigonometric ratios for angles 0° and 90° by considering the limiting behavior of a right-angled triangle. It explains how side lengths change as angle A approaches these extreme values, leading to definitions for sine and cosine at 0° and 90°. Consequently, it shows which other trigonometric ratios become undefined at these angles due to division by zero.

This page presents a table of trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, tangent, cosecant, secant, cotangent) for specific angles: 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°. It highlights how sine and cosine values change as the angle increases from 0° to 90°. An example then illustrates how to use these trigonometric values to calculate unknown side lengths in a right-angled triangle.

This page illustrates the application of trigonometric ratios and the Pythagorean theorem to determine unknown sides and angles in right-angled triangles. It provides worked examples demonstrating how to use sine ratio to find side lengths and angles. Additionally, it shows how to solve a system of trigonometric equations to find the values of two unknown angles.

This page presents Exercise 8.2, which focuses on evaluating trigonometric expressions for specific standard angles (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°). It includes multiple-choice questions testing knowledge of trigonometric identities and values, and problems requiring the application of sum/difference identities. Additionally, it features true/false statements to assess conceptual understanding of trigonometric function properties.

This page introduces the concept of trigonometric identities as equations true for all values of the involved angle. It then proves the first fundamental trigonometric identity, cos² A + sin² A = 1, by dividing the Pythagorean theorem (derived from a right-angled triangle) by AC². The page also derives a second identity, 1 + tan² A = sec² A, by dividing the Pythagorean theorem by AB², highlighting the angle restrictions for which it is valid.

This page introduces the trigonometric identity `cot² A + 1 = cosec² A`, noting its domain restrictions. It then demonstrates how to express various trigonometric ratios (cos A, tan A, sec A, cosec A) in terms of a single known ratio (like sin A or tan A) using these identities. The page includes worked examples for expressing ratios and proving an identity.

This page provides worked examples demonstrating how to prove trigonometric identities. It showcases the transformation of expressions involving cotangent, cosine, cosecant, sine, and tangent into equivalent forms, utilizing fundamental identities like `1 - sin² A = cos² A` and `sec² θ = 1 + tan² θ` along with algebraic manipulation.

This page is an exercise set (Exercise 8.3) focused on fundamental trigonometric concepts and identities. Students are challenged to express trigonometric ratios in terms of others, select correct options for expressions, and prove various trigonometric identities, with some hints provided for complex proofs.

This page summarizes key trigonometric concepts and identities. It defines the basic trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, tangent) in a right-angled triangle, along with their reciprocal relationships and quotient identity. The chapter summary also highlights the three fundamental Pythagorean identities and discusses the range of values for various trigonometric ratios, especially for acute angles.

This chapter introduces real-world applications of trigonometry, specifically focusing on heights and distances. It defines key concepts such as the 'line of sight' as the line from an observer's eye to the object viewed. The 'angle of elevation' is introduced as the angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when an observer looks up at an object.

This page introduces two key trigonometric concepts: the angle of elevation and the angle of depression. The angle of elevation describes the angle formed between the line of sight and the horizontal when an object is viewed above the observer's horizontal level. Conversely, the angle of depression is formed when an object is viewed below the observer's horizontal level, both defined by the line of sight and the horizontal.

This page introduces the application of trigonometric ratios, specifically tan and cot, to solve problems involving heights and distances. It explains how to set up problems by forming right-angled triangles and identifying the knowns and unknowns. A detailed worked example demonstrates how to find the height of a tower given the distance from its foot and the angle of elevation, illustrating the practical use of trigonometry.

This page demonstrates the real-world application of trigonometric ratios to solve a practical problem involving a ladder and a pole. It calculates both the required length of the ladder and the optimal distance to place its foot from the base of the pole, using the sine and cotangent ratios for a given angle of inclination.

This page introduces the application of trigonometry to solve real-world problems involving heights and distances. It uses the concept of the angle of elevation and the tangent trigonometric ratio. Two worked examples are presented to illustrate how to calculate unknown heights and distances by setting up and solving right-angled triangles.

This page demonstrates solving real-world problems involving heights and distances using trigonometric ratios. It presents a worked example of calculating the height of a flagstaff on a building using angles of elevation and then introduces another problem about finding the height of a tower based on changing shadow lengths and angles of elevation.

This page continues the solution of a trigonometry problem, demonstrating how to find the height of a tower using angles of elevation and trigonometric ratios within right triangles. It then introduces a new word problem, 'Example 6', which requires calculating the height of a multi-storeyed building and the distance to another building using angles of depression and similar geometric principles, setting up the problem with a corresponding figure.

This page continues the solution of a trigonometry problem involving the height of a multi-storeyed building and the distance between two buildings, using angles of elevation/depression. It then introduces and begins the solution for a new problem (Example 7) that uses angles of depression from a bridge to find the width of a river.

This page focuses on practical applications of trigonometry, specifically for solving problems involving heights and distances. It presents the concluding steps of a worked example that calculates the width of a river, followed by a set of seven practice problems in 'EXERCISE 9.1'. These problems require students to apply trigonometric ratios to various real-world scenarios, such as finding the height of a pole, a tree, or a tower, and calculating distances or lengths of slides and strings.

This page presents a series of word problems focused on applying trigonometric concepts to calculate heights and distances in various real-world scenarios. The problems involve angles of elevation and depression to determine unknown lengths or heights of objects like statues, buildings, towers, lighthouses, and moving balloons.

This page summarizes fundamental concepts in the applications of trigonometry. It defines the 'line of sight' as the line from an observer's eye to an object, and explains 'angle of elevation' when looking upwards and 'angle of depression' when looking downwards. The summary concludes by stating that trigonometric ratios are essential tools for determining the height, length, or distance between objects.

This introductory page reviews the definition of a circle and related terms from Class IX. It then presents the three possible relationships between a line and a circle in a plane: a non-intersecting line, a secant (intersecting at two points), and a tangent (touching at exactly one point). Each relationship is visually explained through diagrams.

This page introduces the concept of a tangent to a circle, defining it as a line that intersects the circle at exactly one point. Through an activity involving a rotating line around a fixed point on a circular wire, it demonstrates how a tangent emerges from various secant positions. The page concludes by defining a tangent as a special case of a secant where the two end points of its corresponding chord coincide.

This page defines a tangent to a circle as a special case of a secant where the two intersection points coincide, a concept explored through an activity. It introduces the 'point of contact' where the tangent touches the circle. Through a real-world example of a bicycle wheel, the page motivates and formally states Theorem 10.1, which establishes that the radius at the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent.

This page introduces the fundamental property of a tangent to a circle: it is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. It explains that this occurs because the radius represents the shortest distance from the circle's center to the tangent line. Additionally, the page defines the 'normal' to the circle as the line containing the radius at the point of contact and states that only one tangent can exist at any given point on a circle. An exercise set reinforces these geometric concepts.

This page elucidates the concept of tangents to a circle based on the position of an external point P relative to the circle. It demonstrates through an activity that no tangents can be drawn from a point inside the circle, exactly one tangent can be drawn from a point on the circle, and precisely two tangents can be drawn from a point outside the circle. The page also defines the 'length of the tangent' from an external point and poses a question about the equality of the lengths of the two tangents from an external point, hinting at an upcoming theorem.

This page introduces Theorem 10.2, which states that the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. It provides a detailed proof using congruence of triangles (RHS criterion) and offers an alternative proof using the Pythagoras Theorem. The page also highlights that the line segment connecting the external point to the circle's centre bisects the angle between the tangents. An example problem is introduced, demonstrating how to prove that a chord of a larger concentric circle is bisected by the point of contact with the smaller circle.

This page focuses on the properties of tangents to a circle and their relationship with chords and angles. It presents two worked examples demonstrating how to prove an angular relationship between tangents and radii, and how to calculate lengths using properties of tangents, chords, and the Pythagorean theorem. Key theorems regarding tangents and perpendiculars from the center to a chord are applied.

This page demonstrates two methods to calculate the length of a tangent segment using geometric properties. It first uses similar triangles (AA similarity) and then provides an alternative solution using the Pythagorean theorem. Following the explanation, there is an exercise section with three multiple-choice questions related to tangents and their properties in circles.

This page presents a series of problems designed to reinforce understanding of geometric properties related to circles and tangents. It includes exercises requiring proofs about parallel tangents, perpendicularity at the point of contact, and properties of quadrilaterals and triangles circumscribing circles, alongside calculations involving radii and lengths of tangents and chords.

This page provides a summary of key concepts covered in the chapter on Circles. It defines the meaning of a tangent to a circle, states the property that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, and highlights that the lengths of two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

This page introduces the fundamental concepts of sectors and segments of a circle. It defines a sector as the region enclosed by two radii and an arc, differentiating between minor and major sectors based on the central angle. Similarly, it defines a segment as the region enclosed by a chord and an arc, distinguishing between minor and major segments. A remark clarifies that "segment" and "sector" typically refer to their minor counterparts unless specified otherwise.

This page explains how to derive the formulas for the area of a sector and the length of an arc of a circle. It uses the Unitary Method, starting from the known area and circumference of a full circle (corresponding to a 360° angle). The derived formulas relate these quantities to the circle's radius (r) and the sector's central angle (θ in degrees).

This page introduces the formulas for calculating the area of a circular segment and defines major and minor sectors and segments. It provides an example illustrating how to calculate the area of a minor sector and its corresponding major sector using two different methods, given the radius and central angle of a circle.

This page demonstrates how to calculate the area of a circular segment. It presents a worked example that involves finding the area of the corresponding sector and subtracting the area of the inscribed triangle. The solution uses geometric properties and trigonometry to determine the dimensions needed for the triangle's area calculation.

This page concludes a worked example demonstrating the calculation of the area of a triangle and a circular segment. It then introduces Exercise 11.1, which consists of eight problems focused on calculating areas of sectors, quadrants, and segments of circles, as well as arc lengths, using given radii and angles.

This page presents a series of application-based exercises focused on calculating areas related to circles, specifically sectors and segments. Problems involve real-world scenarios like brooches, umbrellas, car wipers, lighthouses, and table covers, requiring students to apply formulas for area, circumference, and sector area in various practical contexts. The page also includes a multiple-choice question to assess understanding of the area of a sector formula.

This page summarizes key formulas related to the geometry of circles. It provides methods for calculating the length of an arc of a sector, the area of a sector, and the area of a segment of a circle. These formulas are presented as a summary of points studied in the chapter.

This introductory page for the chapter "Surface Areas and Volumes" reminds students of their prior knowledge of basic 3D shapes (cuboid, cone, cylinder, sphere) and their surface areas and volumes from Class IX. It then introduces the primary focus of the chapter: analyzing and calculating properties of solids formed by combining two or more of these basic shapes, using a tanker truck as a real-world illustration.

This page introduces the concept of finding the surface area of objects formed by combining two or more basic three-dimensional solids. It emphasizes the strategy of decomposing a complex solid into simpler, known shapes to calculate its surface area. The chapter specifically focuses on calculating the total surface area of such composite solids by summing the curved surface areas of their individual visible components, illustrated with examples like a test tube (cylinder and hemisphere) and a capsule-like object (cylinder with two hemispheres).

This page introduces the method for calculating the surface area of composite solids formed by joining basic 3D shapes. It explains that for a toy made of a cone and a hemisphere joined at their bases, the total surface area to be colored is the sum of the curved surface areas of the hemisphere and the cone. A worked example demonstrates this concept by finding the area to be colored on a toy lattu (top) with given dimensions.

This page explains how to calculate the surface area of composite solids by combining the surface areas of their individual parts. It highlights the important principle that overlapping or internal surfaces are not part of the total exposed surface area of the new solid. An example illustrates this by calculating the total surface area of a decorative block made from a cube topped with a hemisphere.

This page illustrates how to calculate the surface areas of composite solids, specifically a toy rocket shaped as a cone mounted on a cylinder. It demonstrates the process of identifying individual surfaces to be painted and applying relevant geometric formulas, including the special case of a base ring area when one component rests on another of a different base size. The example focuses on calculating the area to be painted with two different colors.

This page introduces the concept of finding the total surface area of composite solids by providing a worked example of a bird-bath (cylinder with a hemispherical depression). It then presents Exercise 12.1, which consists of six practice problems requiring students to calculate surface areas of various combinations of 3D shapes such as cubes, cylinders, hemispheres, and cones, often requiring careful consideration of joined surfaces.

This page continues with problem-solving for the surface areas of combined solids, featuring a tent, a cylinder with a conical cavity, and a wooden article with hemispherical scoops. It then introduces the concept of calculating the volume of combined solids, explicitly stating that volumes are always additive, unlike surface areas where common parts might disappear. An example demonstrates calculating the available air volume in an industrial shed (cuboid with a half-cylinder roof) after accounting for machinery and workers.

This page provides worked examples on calculating volumes of composite solids. It demonstrates how to find the air volume in a shed constructed from a cuboid and a half-cylinder, accounting for occupied space. Additionally, it illustrates determining the apparent and actual capacity of a cylindrical glass containing a hemispherical raised base.

This page focuses on calculating volumes of composite solids, specifically those formed by combining basic 3D shapes like hemispheres, cones, and cylinders. It provides a detailed worked example to find the volume of a toy (hemisphere surmounted by a cone) and the difference between its volume and that of a circumscribing cylinder. The page concludes with practice exercises for students to apply these concepts to similar real-world scenarios.

This page presents a series of exercises focused on calculating the surface areas and volumes of various objects formed by combining basic three-dimensional solids like cuboids, cones, cylinders, spheres, and hemispheres. It concludes with a summary reiterating that the chapter covers methods to determine both surface area and volume for such combined shapes. The problems involve practical scenarios like finding the volume of syrup in sweets or the volume of wood in a pen stand.

This page introduces the Class 10 Statistics chapter, reviewing concepts from Class 9 such as classification of data into ungrouped and grouped frequency distributions, and pictorial representations like bar graphs and histograms. It highlights the focus of the current chapter on extending measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) to grouped data, and introducing cumulative frequency and ogives. The page then specifically defines and provides the formula for calculating the mean of grouped data.

This page introduces the formula for calculating the mean of data when individual observations are associated with frequencies. It presents the formula for the mean (x-bar) using summation notation. A detailed worked example demonstrates how to apply this formula to find the mean marks obtained by students in a mathematics paper, by organizing the data in a frequency table and calculating the necessary sums.

This page explains the necessity of converting ungrouped data into grouped data for meaningful study, especially with large datasets. It details the process of forming class intervals and the convention for allocating frequencies when a data point matches an upper class limit. The page also introduces the concept of a 'class mark' (mid-point) as a representative value for each class interval, providing a formula for its calculation to prepare for computing the mean of grouped data.

This page introduces the Direct Method for calculating the mean of grouped data, utilizing class intervals, frequencies, and class marks. It demonstrates the calculation with an example and explains that this method yields an approximate mean due to the mid-point assumption. The page then transitions to the Assumed Mean Method, detailing how subtracting a fixed number ('a', the assumed mean) from each class mark ('x_i') to obtain 'd_i' can simplify calculations, especially when dealing with large numbers.

This page explains the assumed mean method for calculating the mean of grouped data. It details how to calculate deviations from an assumed mean, form a product with frequencies, and sum these values. The page then mathematically derives the relationship between the true mean and the mean of deviations, culminating in the formula for the mean using this method.

This page reviews the Assumed Mean Method for calculating the mean of grouped data, illustrating how the mean remains constant regardless of the chosen 'a'. It then introduces the Step-Deviation Method as an extension, defining a new variable `u_i = (x_i - a) / h` to simplify calculations, and presents a comprehensive table (Table 13.5) detailing the computations for this method. The page concludes by setting up the formula for the mean of `u_i` values.

This page explains the step-deviation method for calculating the mean of grouped data. It derives the formula for the mean (x̄ = a + hū) starting from the definition of u_i = (x_i - a) / h and the mean of u_i (ū).
