The page also highlights key properties of the step-deviation method, noting its convenience when deviations have a common factor and confirming that all three methods (direct, assumed mean, step-deviation) yield the same mean.

This page introduces an example problem to calculate the mean percentage of female teachers from a grouped frequency distribution. It demonstrates the initial step of finding the class marks (x_i) for each class interval. The page also sets up the parameters 'a' (assumed mean) and 'h' (class size) for subsequent calculations using the assumed mean and step-deviation methods.

This page demonstrates three methods for calculating the mean of grouped data: the direct method, the assumed mean method, and the step-deviation method. It uses an example dataset of female teachers' percentages across states to illustrate each calculation, showing that all three methods yield the same result. A remark explains when to use each method based on the numerical values of the data.

This page demonstrates the calculation of the mean for grouped data using the step-deviation method. It addresses a scenario where class sizes vary and class marks are large, providing a detailed example from cricket statistics and explaining the significance of the calculated mean.

This page introduces practical activities for students to collect and organize data into grouped frequency distributions. It then provides exercises that require calculating the mean from grouped frequency tables in various real-world contexts, including a problem to find a missing frequency given the overall mean.

This page provides four distinct exercises focused on calculating the mean for grouped data presented in frequency distribution tables. Students are required to apply suitable statistical methods to find the mean in various real-world contexts, including medical readings, market distribution, household expenditures, and environmental data. The problems reinforce the concept of measures of central tendency for class-interval data.

This page introduces the concept of the mode for grouped data, building upon the understanding of mode for ungrouped data from Class IX. It explains that the mode is the observation with the maximum frequency and clarifies that while data can be multimodal, the focus here will be on problems with a single mode. The page also includes exercises on calculating the mean for grouped data and a worked example demonstrating how to find the mode for ungrouped data by forming a frequency distribution table.

This page explains how to calculate the mode for grouped frequency distributions. It defines the modal class as the class with the highest frequency and introduces the formula for calculating the mode, along with definitions for all its variables. A worked example demonstrates the application of this formula using real-world survey data on family sizes.

This page focuses on calculating the mode for grouped frequency data using a specific formula. It provides a detailed worked example (Example 6) that demonstrates the application of the formula to find the mode of student marks and interprets its value in comparison to the mean. The page also includes remarks on the possible relationship between mode and mean.

This page introduces Exercise 13.2, which consists of three problems focused on calculating and interpreting the mean and mode for grouped data. Students are required to apply these statistical measures to real-world datasets such as patient ages, electrical component lifetimes, and household expenditures.

This page provides three practice exercises related to statistics, specifically focusing on grouped frequency distributions. Students are asked to calculate the mode for all distributions and the mean for one, applying the relevant formulas and interpreting the results. The problems involve real-world data like teacher-student ratios, cricket runs, and car traffic frequency.

This page introduces the concept of the median for grouped data, starting with a recall of how the median is calculated for ungrouped data. It explains the median as the middle-most observation, outlining distinct formulas for when the total number of observations ('n') is odd or even. An example problem is then presented, demonstrating the initial step of arranging given marks into an ascending frequency table.

This page explains how to determine the median for a data set when the total number of observations (n) is an even number, by averaging the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th observations. It illustrates this concept with an example involving student marks and the calculation of cumulative frequency. The page demonstrates the step-by-step computation of cumulative frequencies and presents a consolidated cumulative frequency table.

This page introduces the concept of the median, demonstrating its calculation for an ungrouped dataset and explaining its interpretation as the point that divides data into two equal halves. It then prepares the reader for finding the median of grouped data by presenting a grouped frequency distribution table (Table 13.12) showing student marks. A simple question about reading the table is also provided with its answer.

This page introduces the concept of cumulative frequency in statistics, specifically focusing on the "less than" type cumulative frequency distribution. It explains how to calculate the cumulative frequency for various class intervals by summing the frequencies of preceding classes. Table 13.13 provides a detailed example of this calculation for student marks, and the text also briefly explains the derivation of "more than or equal to" cumulative frequencies.

This page explains and illustrates different types of cumulative frequency distributions. It presents a 'more than type' cumulative frequency table (Table 13.14) and demonstrates how its values are derived. Subsequently, it shows how a standard class interval frequency distribution with 'less than type' cumulative frequencies (Table 13.15) is constructed, noting that both types are useful for finding the median of grouped data.

This page explains the method for calculating the median of grouped data. It details how to identify the 'median class' by finding the class whose cumulative frequency is greater than and nearest to half the total number of observations. The formula for the median, involving the lower limit of the median class, cumulative frequency of the preceding class, frequency of the median class, and class size, is then presented and demonstrated with a worked example.

This page introduces the process of converting a 'less than' type cumulative frequency distribution into a standard frequency distribution table with class intervals and individual frequencies. It presents a worked example where height data for girls is transformed from a cumulative format, preparing it for subsequent calculations like finding the median.

This page demonstrates the calculation of the median for grouped data using a specific formula. It first provides a worked example showing how to apply the formula to find the median height from a given frequency distribution. Subsequently, it introduces a problem where the median and total frequency are known, and two missing frequencies within a frequency distribution table need to be determined.

This page demonstrates how to find missing frequencies (denoted as 'x' and 'y') in a grouped frequency distribution. It uses the given total frequency and median value, along with the formula for the median of grouped data, to set up and solve a system of linear equations. The solution involves calculating the class boundaries, cumulative frequencies, and applying algebraic steps to determine the unknown frequencies.

This page discusses the appropriate situations for using mean, median, and mode as measures of central tendency. It highlights that the mean is sensitive to extreme values, making the median more suitable for typical observations in such cases, while the mode is best for identifying the most frequent item. The page also presents an empirical relationship that connects these three statistical measures.

This page, part of Exercise 13.3, provides practice problems on statistical analysis of grouped data. Students are asked to calculate mean, median, and mode from given frequency distributions, and to find missing frequencies when the median is known. The problems are set in real-world contexts such as electricity consumption and life insurance policy data.

This page introduces grouped data representation through two tables: one showing the cumulative distribution of policyholders by age, and another showing the frequency distribution of leaf lengths. It includes an exercise requiring the calculation of the median for the leaf length data, with a specific hint emphasizing the necessity of converting discrete class intervals into continuous classes before applying the median formula for grouped data.

This page provides practice exercises for calculating the median, mean, and mode from grouped frequency distribution tables. It concludes with a summary of the formulas for calculating the mean of grouped data, specifically the direct method and the assumed mean method.

This page defines the step deviation method for calculating the mean, provides formulas for finding the mode and median of grouped data, and explains the concept of cumulative frequency. It emphasizes the importance of ensuring continuous class intervals before applying these statistical formulas or constructing ogives.

This page introduces the concept of probability and its theoretical approach, defining essential terms. It explains what constitutes a 'fair' or 'unbiased' coin or die and clarifies the meaning of a 'random toss'. Through examples of coin tosses and die rolls, the concept of 'equally likely outcomes' is illustrated.

This page introduces the concept of equally likely outcomes in probability, clarifying that while not all experiments naturally have them, this chapter will proceed with that assumption. It revisits the definition of experimental probability and discusses its practical limitations, particularly for events that are hard to repeat. Finally, it formally defines theoretical probability (also called classical probability) as the ratio of favorable outcomes to total possible outcomes, under the assumption of equally likely outcomes, attributing this definition to Pierre Simon Laplace.

This page introduces the origins of probability theory, crediting mathematicians like Cardan and Laplace, and highlights its widespread applications in various fields. It then lays the foundation for calculating probability for events with equally likely outcomes. The fundamental formula is explained and demonstrated through basic examples involving coin tosses and drawing balls from a bag.

This page introduces the concept of an elementary event in probability, defined as an event with only one outcome. It demonstrates how to calculate the probability of elementary events using examples involving colored balls and a die roll. A key property highlighted is that the sum of the probabilities of all elementary events in an experiment is always equal to 1.

This page introduces the concept of complementary events in probability, demonstrating through examples that the sum of the probabilities of an event and its complement is always 1. It defines the complement of an event, denoted as E-bar, and provides the formula P(E-bar) = 1 - P(E). The page also begins discussing the probability of an impossible event with a worked example of rolling an 8 on a standard die.

This page defines impossible events (probability 0) and sure events (probability 1), establishing that the probability of any event P(E) must fall within the range 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. It also provides a detailed example of calculating probabilities for specific events (drawing an ace) and its complement (not drawing an ace) from a deck of playing cards.

This page introduces and reinforces the concept of complementary events in probability. It explains how to calculate the probability of an event's complement using the formula P(E̅) = 1 - P(E). This concept is then applied through worked examples, demonstrating its use in scenarios such as calculating the probability of one player winning a match given the other's winning probability, and determining the probability of two friends having different or the same birthdays.

This page introduces the fundamental concept of calculating the probability of an event. It demonstrates how to find probability by dividing the number of favourable outcomes by the total number of possible outcomes through two detailed examples. The page also illustrates the principle of complementary events and that the sum of probabilities of all elementary events in an experiment equals 1.

This page introduces fundamental concepts of probability through a detailed example of tossing two coins, demonstrating how to determine sample space, favorable outcomes, and calculate probability, including using the complement rule. It then highlights the limitation of this traditional probability definition for experiments with infinitely many outcomes, setting the stage for continuous probability concepts. A new example is introduced to illustrate situations where outcomes are continuous, such as time intervals.

This page introduces the concept of probability for events in a continuous sample space, first by calculating the probability based on the ratio of favorable distance to total distance. It then extends this idea to geometric probability, where the probability of an event is determined by the ratio of a favorable area to the total possible area, illustrated with an example involving a helicopter crash in a lake.

This page introduces basic probability concepts through worked examples. It demonstrates how to calculate the probability of an event by determining the number of favorable outcomes and dividing by the total number of possible outcomes. Examples involve calculating probabilities in scenarios such as product defect analysis and outcomes when rolling two dice.

This page demonstrates how to determine the sample space for experiments involving rolling two dice and subsequently calculate the probabilities of various events. It presents a detailed table of all possible outcomes and uses this table to illustrate the calculation of probabilities for an event with a specific sum (sum of 8), an impossible event (sum of 13), and a sure event (sum less than or equal to 12). The importance of ordered pairs in defining the sample space is also highlighted.

This page presents a comprehensive exercise set (Exercise 14.1) focusing on fundamental concepts of probability. It covers definitions of probability, properties of events (impossible, certain, complementary), and calculations involving equally likely outcomes in various real-world scenarios. Students are expected to apply basic probability rules and definitions to solve problems.

This page provides a series of practice problems designed to reinforce fundamental probability concepts. Students are required to calculate probabilities for various real-world scenarios, including selecting items from a collection (coins, fish, cards, pens, bulbs, numbered discs) and determining outcomes of games of chance (spinner, die). The exercises cover basic probability calculations as well as scenarios involving conditional probability with changes in the sample space.

This page provides a set of practice exercises on probability, covering various scenarios such as outcomes from custom dice, geometric probability, defective items, coin tosses, and sums from rolling two dice. It also includes a critical thinking question challenging a common misconception about equally likely outcomes in probability.

This page summarizes key concepts in theoretical probability, including its definition based on favorable and total outcomes, properties like the probability range (0 to 1) and the probabilities of sure and impossible events. It also defines elementary and complementary events, and includes an exercise to assess understanding of probability calculations and common misconceptions regarding sample spaces and equally likely outcomes.

This page introduces the concept of proofs in mathematics, emphasizing the importance of clear reasoning. It highlights how faulty reasoning can be misleading in daily life and in mathematics. The chapter will review mathematical statements, deductive reasoning, negation, converse, and proof by contradiction, building upon concepts learned in Class IX.

This page introduces the fundamental concept of a 'statement' in mathematics, distinguishing it from questions, orders, and exclamations. It defines three types of statements: 'always true,' 'always false,' and 'ambiguous.' Crucially, it clarifies that for a sentence to be considered an 'acceptable mathematical statement,' it must be either always true or always false, thus excluding ambiguous sentences.

This page demonstrates how to evaluate and justify the truth value of mathematical statements across various topics, including properties of numbers (rational, integers) and basic geometric principles (triangles, quadrilaterals). It also includes an exercise that challenges students to refine given statements by adding appropriate conditions to make them mathematically true.

This page introduces the concept of proofs in mathematics, providing examples of mathematical statements and how they can be restated. It includes an exercise set focused on evaluating the truthfulness, ambiguity, and conditions of various mathematical and general statements. The page also begins a discussion on deductive reasoning.

This page introduces the fundamental concept of deductive reasoning in mathematics. It explains that conclusions are derived from given statements, known as 'premises' or 'hypotheses', which are assumed to be true for the purpose of deduction. Various examples from different branches of mathematics illustrate how to apply this reasoning process.

This page introduces the principles of deductive reasoning in mathematics, emphasizing that the validity of the reasoning process is paramount, regardless of the truthfulness of the initial hypotheses. It highlights that incorrect premises can lead to flawed conclusions. The content includes an exercise set (A1.2) focused on logical deduction and an introduction to conjectures through an activity (A1.4) involving the division of a circle by connecting points.

This page explains the difference between a mathematical conjecture and a proven statement, emphasizing that verifying a pattern for several cases is not sufficient for proof. It uses the example of regions formed by connecting points on a circle, where a seemingly correct conjecture (2^(n-1) regions) fails for n=6 and n=7. The text highlights the importance of counter-examples in disproving mathematical statements and the necessity of formal proof for establishing truth.

This page introduces the concept of mathematical proofs, explaining that a proof consists of a sequence of valid arguments based on previous statements, axioms, definitions, or assumptions, leading to a logical conclusion. It specifically focuses on the 'direct' or 'deductive' method of proof. An example is provided to illustrate this method by proving that the sum of two rational numbers is also a rational number, detailing each step and its justification.

This page first concludes a proof demonstrating that the sum of two rational numbers is rational, leveraging properties of integers. Subsequently, it presents a detailed worked example, "Example 11," which proves that every prime number greater than 3 must be of the form 6k + 1 or 6k + 5. The proof utilizes Euclid's division lemma and a method called "Proof by Exhaustion" to systematically eliminate other possibilities.

This page introduces and provides a detailed proof for the Converse of the Pythagoras Theorem. The theorem states that if the square of the length of one side of a triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides, then the angle opposite the first side is a right angle. The proof uses geometric construction, the original Pythagoras Theorem, and triangle congruence (SSS criterion) to establish the conclusion.

The page begins with Exercise A1.3, presenting six problems that require students to prove mathematical statements across various topics including number theory, properties of rational numbers, Euclid's Division Lemma, and basic geometry (Basic Proportionality Theorem). Subsequently, Section A1.5 introduces the fundamental concept of 'Negation of a Statement' and demonstrates a formal notation for representing simple statements using variables (e.g., p, q, r).

This page introduces the concept of negation of statements, denoted by '~p' for a statement 'p', illustrating its formation using a table of examples. It emphasizes that a negation means 'It is false that...' before the original statement. A crucial point is made about the common misconception of simply inserting 'not', especially with statements involving 'all', and provides guidance for correct negation, stating that a statement and its negation must always have opposite truth values.

This page introduces the concept of negation for mathematical statements, explaining how to form the opposite truth value of a given statement. It demonstrates negation with simple statements, double negation, and statements involving quantifiers like 'All' and 'Some'. A working rule is provided to guide students in correctly negating various types of statements, emphasizing proper modification for universal and existential quantifiers.

This page introduces the concept of negation for various types of mathematical and general statements through an exercise. It then delves into the structure of conditional statements, explaining how 'if-then' constructs form compound statements from simple ones, identifying the hypothesis and conclusion. Finally, the page defines the 'converse' of a conditional statement as one formed by interchanging its hypothesis and conclusion.

This page introduces the concept of the converse of a conditional statement. It explains that for a statement 'p implies q', its converse is 'q implies p'. The page provides multiple examples, some mathematical and some general, to illustrate how to form the converse of various statements. It also highlights an important point: the truth value of the converse is not necessarily the same as the original statement.

This page introduces the concept of the 'converse' of a mathematical statement, denoted as `q => p` when the original statement is `p => q`. It explains that even if the original statement is true, its converse may or may not be true. The page provides several examples from number theory and geometry to illustrate how to form converses and determine their truth value, followed by practice exercises.

This page introduces the concept of converses of mathematical statements, requiring the reader to determine their truth values. It then delves into 'Proof by Contradiction' as a powerful indirect argument method, defining what a contradiction is in mathematics. The text explains the mechanism of contradiction using an example related to rational numbers and outlines a simple logical example to illustrate the method's application.

This page introduces the method of proof by contradiction, demonstrating its general application with a logical argument. It then applies this technique to a mathematical problem (Example 15), proving that the product of a non-zero rational number and an irrational number is irrational, with a step-by-step explanation in a table format.

This page illustrates the proof by contradiction method through two examples. It first outlines a partial proof for an irrational number, and then fully details Example 11. Example 11 uses Euclid's division lemma to prove that every prime number greater than 3 must be of the form 6n + 1 or 6n + 5.

This page introduces Theorem A1.2, which states that the shortest distance from an external point to a line is the perpendicular segment. It then provides a detailed proof for this theorem using the method of contradiction, explaining each step and its justification. The proof involves geometric constructions and relies on the property that the side of a right triangle is less than its hypotenuse.

This page presents a set of exercises focusing on proof by contradiction, covering various topics like number properties, rationality, and basic geometry. It also includes a summary of key concepts discussed in Appendix A1, such as different elements of a proof, negation, converse of a statement, and the proof by contradiction method itself.

This page introduces the concept of mathematical modelling, defining it as the process of creating a mathematical description of a real-life situation to analyze and solve problems. It explains the steps involved, from converting a real-world problem into a mathematical one, solving it, interpreting the solution, and validating the model. Several examples from various domains are provided to illustrate the broad applicability and importance of mathematical modelling.

This page introduces the concept of mathematical modelling, emphasizing its role in solving real-world problems. It outlines the first two critical stages: 'Understanding the problem,' which involves defining, discussing, and simplifying the problem, and 'Mathematical description and formulation,' where the problem's aspects are translated into mathematical terms using variables, equations, data, graphs, or probabilities. The text also provides several real-world scenarios where mathematical modelling can be applied.

This page details Steps 3, 4, and 5 of the mathematical modelling process using an example of estimating fish population in a lake. Step 3 involves solving the simplified mathematical problem, which is demonstrated with a ratio and proportion calculation. Step 4 focuses on interpreting the mathematical solution in the real-world context, and Step 5 explains how to validate the model and revise assumptions if the results don't make sense or new information arises.

This page illustrates the iterative process of mathematical modeling using a flowchart. It outlines steps from defining a real-life problem, simplifying it, describing it mathematically, and solving it, to interpreting and validating the solution. The process emphasizes that if a solution doesn't adequately capture the real-life situation, assumptions must be changed, highlighting the balance between simplification and accuracy in model development.

This page introduces the classic Fibonacci rabbit problem as an example of mathematical modelling. It describes the assumptions for rabbit reproduction and presents a table illustrating the monthly growth of rabbit pairs according to the Fibonacci sequence. The page concludes with an exercise prompting students to articulate the problem and identify the stages of mathematical modelling involved.

This page introduces the concept of mathematical modeling by applying it to a probability problem: guessing the sum of two dice. It outlines a three-step process involving understanding the problem, describing it mathematically by listing all possible outcomes, and solving it by calculating probabilities for each sum. The example concludes by identifying the sum with the highest probability (7) as the best guess.

This page continues a discussion on mathematical modelling by outlining Step 4 (interpreting a solution based on probability, e.g., guessing the highest probability outcome) and Step 5 (validating a model by comparing observed frequencies to theoretical probabilities). It then provides extensive background for an upcoming mathematical modelling problem, introducing the concept of "instalment schemes" as a method for purchasing goods. Key financial terms like "cash price," "cash down payment," and "deferred payment" are defined, with a note on simple interest for payments made within one year. The page also touches upon the historical perception of charging interest.

This page presents a worked example demonstrating how to compare two financial options for purchasing an item: an instalment scheme offered by a shopkeeper and a bank loan with simple interest. It outlines a step-by-step process to calculate the effective interest rate charged in the instalment scheme. The ultimate goal is to determine the more economical choice by comparing the interest rates.

This page begins with a problem involving financial calculations related to purchasing a television using either cash or an installment plan with simple interest. Following this, it delves into the significance of mathematical modelling. It explains how modelling aids in understanding real-world systems, predicting future outcomes, forecasting, and simulating scenarios, providing several practical examples.

This page introduces the concept of mathematical modelling, emphasizing its utility in estimating large values and predicting real-world outcomes, such as election results or academic performance. It also summarizes the key components of mathematical modelling, including its definition as a description of real-life situations, the step-by-step process of creating and using models, and the overall importance of this approach.

This page provides answers and hints for exercises from various chapters, including number theory (prime factorization, LCM, HCF), polynomials (number of zeroes, finding zeroes, and forming quadratic polynomials), and pairs of linear equations in two variables (graphical solutions). It serves as a solution key for students to check their understanding and solutions.

This page provides answers and hints for previous exercises related to pairs of linear equations, covering topics like graphical representation, types of solutions (unique, infinite, no solution), and system consistency. It then introduces 'EXERCISE 3.2', which consists of practice problems that require students to solve systems of linear equations, often formulated from various real-world scenarios such as costs, ages, and geometric properties.

This page contains exercises and their solutions from two distinct chapters of a mathematics textbook: Chapter 3 (Linear Equations) and Chapter 4 (Quadratic Equations). Exercise 3.3 focuses on solving systems of linear equations and formulating them from diverse word problems involving real-world scenarios. Exercises 4.1 and 4.2 deal with quadratic equations, requiring students to identify their nature, formulate them from word problems, and find their solutions.

This page provides answers and hints for exercises from Chapter 4 (Quadratic Equations) and Chapter 5 (Arithmetic Progressions). It lists solutions for determining the nature of roots, finding coefficients for given root conditions, and solving word problems related to quadratic equations. For Arithmetic Progressions, it provides answers for identifying APs, listing their terms, and finding initial terms or common differences.

This page provides a set of solutions or answers to an unstated previous exercise (numbered 2-20) and presents 'EXERCISE 5.3' which focuses on problems related to Arithmetic Progressions (AP). The exercise includes a worked example demonstrating how to use the sum of AP formula to derive and solve a quadratic equation, as well as numerous practice problems for calculating sums, terms, and various parameters of an AP.

This page serves as an answer key and provides detailed hints for exercises from Chapters 5 (Arithmetic Progressions) and 6 (Triangles). It includes key formulas for terms and sums of APs, a worked example demonstrating problem-solving in AP with real-world context, and solutions or hints for problems involving properties of similar triangles and geometric constructions.

This page serves as an answer key for three distinct exercises: Exercise 7.1, Exercise 7.2, and Exercise 8.1. The answers cover topics in coordinate geometry, including distance formulas, classification of quadrilaterals, section formula, and area calculations. It also provides answers for introductory trigonometry, such as trigonometric ratios and true/false statements regarding trigonometric identities.

This page serves as an answer key or hints section for various exercises from Chapters 8, 9, and 10 of a mathematics textbook. It provides numerical answers, trigonometric identities, and categorical responses for problems spanning trigonometry and geometry topics.

This page provides the solutions to various problems from three different exercises: Exercise 11.1, Exercise 12.1, and Exercise 12.2, all pertaining to geometric measurements. The problems involve calculating areas, volumes, and related quantities of various shapes, sometimes including composite solids or real-world contexts like the volume of air in a model. One problem also includes the derivation of a formula for the volume of a composite solid.

This page provides answers and hints for exercises from three chapters: Statistics (Exercises 13.1, 13.2, 13.3) and Probability (Exercise 14.1). The answers cover calculations of mean, median, mode, probabilities, and conceptual understanding of statistical and probability terms.

This page provides solutions and explanations for various probability-related exercises. It includes numerical answers for calculating probabilities, a table detailing probabilities for sums rolled on two dice, and detailed explanations concerning the concept of equally likely outcomes in probability experiments involving coins and dice.

This page provides answers and hints for various exercises (A1.1, A1.2, A1.3, A1.4) covering a range of topics. It includes solutions to true/false statements, properties of real numbers, algebraic identities, and basic geometry facts. The page also offers guidance for logical reasoning problems, particularly those involving the nature of irrational numbers.

This page presents solutions and instructions for various exercises across different sections (A1.5, A1.6, A2.2, A2.3). It covers topics such as logical reasoning with conditional statements, properties of numbers and geometric shapes (triangles, parallelograms, circles), basic arithmetic, and real-world applications involving area, density, and financial calculations. The page serves as a review or answer key for previously introduced concepts.

Fig. 6.1: The image displays two sets of triangles labeled (iii). One set shows two concentric equilateral triangles, and the other set shows two separate equilateral triangles of different sizes. This illustrates that all equilateral triangles, regardless of their size, are similar figures.

Fig. 6.3: The image presents three photographs of the Taj Mahal, each progressively smaller than the last. All three images depict the same monument but are scaled differently. This visually demonstrates the concept of similar figures in real-world contexts, where the shape and proportions are maintained despite changes in size.

Fig. 6.4: A diagram illustrates an activity where a light bulb at point O casts a shadow of a quadrilateral ABCD onto a table, creating an enlarged shadow A'B'C'D'. This setup demonstrates how an enlargement or magnification, such as a shadow, creates a figure that is similar to the original object, maintaining its shape but changing its size.

Fig. 6.5: The image shows two quadrilaterals, ABCD and PQRS, with their side lengths and angle measures explicitly labeled. Quadrilateral ABCD has sides 2.1, 2.4, 2.5, 1.5 cm and angles 85°, 70°, 100°, 105°. Quadrilateral PQRS has sides 4.2, 4.8, 5.0, 3.0 cm and angles 85°, 70°, 100°, 105°. This visual allows for a direct comparison to verify the conditions for similarity, namely that corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are proportional.

Fig. 6.6: This image shows two quadrilaterals: a square ABCD with all sides measuring 3 cm and a rectangle PQRS with sides measuring 3 cm and 3.5 cm. Both figures have all interior angles as right angles (90 degrees). A learner should notice that while all corresponding angles are equal, the ratios of corresponding sides (e.g., AB/PQ = 3/3.5, but BC/QR = 3/3) are not equal, demonstrating that equal corresponding angles alone are not sufficient for two polygons to be similar.

Fig. 6.7: This image displays two quadrilaterals: a square ABCD with all sides measuring 2.1 cm, and a rhombus PQRS with all sides measuring 4.2 cm. A learner should observe that all sides of the rhombus are proportional to the sides of the square (with a ratio of 2:1), but the angles are clearly not equal (the square has 90-degree angles, while the rhombus has acute and obtuse angles). This illustrates that proportional corresponding sides alone are not sufficient for two polygons to be similar.

Fig. 6.8: This image presents two quadrilaterals for comparison: a square ABCD with all sides measuring 3 cm, and a rhombus PQRS with all sides measuring 1.5 cm. The square has all right angles, while the rhombus has acute and obtuse angles. A learner should notice that neither the corresponding angles are equal nor are the sides proportional in a way that matches corresponding angles (as the angles are different). This leads to the conclusion that these figures are not similar, as presented in an exercise asking to determine similarity.

Fig. 6.9: This image shows a geometric construction featuring an angle XAY. Points D and B are marked on ray AX, and points E and C are marked on ray AY. A line segment DE is drawn parallel to another line segment BC. A learner should observe the arrangement of these points and parallel lines, which is a common setup for demonstrating or proving the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT), showing how a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally.

Fig. 6.10: This image displays a triangle ABC with a line segment DE drawn parallel to side BC, intersecting side AB at D and side AC at E. Additional construction lines include BE, CD, and perpendiculars DM to AC and EN to AB. A learner should recognize this as the standard diagram used for proving the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT) or Thales's Theorem, which states that if a line parallel to one side of a triangle intersects the other two sides, then it divides the two sides proportionally.

Fig. 6.11: This image illustrates a geometric construction where two rays, AX and AY, originate from point A. Points B1, B2, B3, B4 are marked at equal distances along ray AX, and points C1, C2, C3, C4 are marked along ray AY such that B1C1, B2C2, B3C3, B4C4 are parallel segments. A learner should notice how the parallel lines divide the segments on the rays proportionally, demonstrating the concept of similar triangles or Thales's Theorem in a constructive way.

Fig. 6.13: This image displays a triangle ABC with a line segment DE drawn parallel to side BC, intersecting sides AB and AC at points D and E respectively. A learner should observe how the parallel line DE divides the other two sides AB and AC proportionally, which is the core concept of the Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT) or Thales's Theorem.

Fig. 6.14: This image presents a trapezium ABCD where sides AB and DC are parallel. A line segment EF is drawn parallel to AB, connecting the non-parallel sides AD and BC at points E and F, respectively. This figure introduces a scenario where the Basic Proportionality Theorem might be applied within a larger shape, requiring students to consider auxiliary constructions.

Fig. 6.15: This image shows the same trapezium ABCD as before, but with an added diagonal AC that intersects the line segment EF at point G. This construction breaks down the trapezium into two triangles (ADC and ABC), allowing the application of the Basic Proportionality Theorem in each triangle independently. A learner should notice how an auxiliary line can simplify a complex shape into components where known theorems can be applied.

Fig. 6.16: This image displays a triangle PQR with a line segment ST connecting points on sides PQ and PR. The problem statement refers to proportional sides and angles within this configuration. A learner should focus on the arrangement of points and segments to analyze similarity conditions, particularly for proving PQR is an isosceles triangle based on given conditions related to ST.

Fig. 6.24: This diagram shows triangle ABC and a larger triangle DEF, with a dashed line segment PQ constructed inside DEF. Learners should observe that the sides of triangle DEF are 1.5 times the corresponding sides of triangle ABC (e.g., 4.5/3 = 1.5, 9/6 = 1.5, 12/8 = 1.5), demonstrating that their corresponding sides are proportional, which is a condition for similarity.

This setup is typically used in proofs to establish a relationship between triangle ABC and triangle DPQ, often to demonstrate the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) or Side-Side-Side (SSS) similarity criterion by showing congruence between ABC and DPQ.

Fig. 7.8: This visual displays a grid representing a classroom with 'Columns' on the x-axis and 'Rows' on the y-axis. Four points, A(3,4), B(6,7), C(9,4), and D(6,1), are marked, forming a quadrilateral. Learners should notice how to accurately read and interpret coordinates on a grid to visualize the relative positions of multiple points and the shape they form.

Fig. 7.11: This diagram illustrates the trisection of a line segment AB by points P and Q. A learner should notice that points P and Q divide the line segment into three equal parts, meaning AP = PQ = QB. This visual helps in understanding the concept of dividing a line segment in a given ratio, specifically for trisection.

Fig. 7.12: This diagram displays a rectangular school ground as a coordinate grid, with flower pots along the y-axis and numbered lines along the x-axis, representing different positions. The image helps visualize distances and relative positions within a coordinate system.

Fig. 8.1: This diagram shows a person observing the top of the Qutub Minar, with dotted lines forming a right-angled triangle. A learner should notice how this real-world scenario can be abstracted into a geometric shape (a right triangle) to apply trigonometric principles for finding unknown heights. The right angle is implicitly formed at the base of the Minar, assuming the ground is level.

Fig. 8.2: This diagram depicts a girl on a balcony looking down at a flower pot on the opposite bank of a river, illustrating a real-world application of trigonometry. A learner should observe how the line of sight, the height of the balcony above the water, and the width of the river form a right-angled triangle, useful for calculating unknown distances or heights. The right angle is formed between the vertical height and the horizontal river width.

Fig. 8.3: This diagram illustrates a hot air balloon moving from position A to B, observed by a person on the ground, creating two right-angled triangles. A learner should notice how the changing position of the balloon affects the angle of elevation and how multiple right triangles can be used to model and solve problems involving varying distances and heights. The common horizontal baseline from the observer to the points directly below the balloons is important for calculations.

Fig. 8.4: This visual shows a right-angled triangle ABC with the right angle at B. It explicitly labels the hypotenuse, the side opposite to angle A (BC), and the side adjacent to angle A (AB), helping learners identify the correct sides relative to a specific acute angle.

Fig. 8.5: This visual displays a right-angled triangle ABC, similar to the previous figure, but with labels relative to angle C. It demonstrates how the labels for 'side opposite' and 'side adjacent' shift when the reference angle changes from A to C, emphasizing that these definitions are angle-dependent.

Fig. 8.6: This visual features a right-angled triangle ABC with additional points P, M, N, and Q, illustrating how similar right-angled triangles can be formed within or extending from the original triangle. It implicitly suggests that trigonometric ratios for a given angle remain constant regardless of the triangle's size, provided the triangles are similar.

Fig. 8.7: This visual presents a right-angled triangle ABC where the side opposite angle A (BC) is labeled 'k' and the hypotenuse (AC) is labeled '3k'. This diagram helps learners understand how to set up trigonometric ratios when side lengths are expressed in terms of a common constant 'k', providing a visual foundation for solving related problems.

Fig. 8.8: This visual displays a right-angled triangle ABC with the side opposite angle A labeled '4k' and the side adjacent to angle A labeled '3k'. This diagram reinforces the concept of proportional side lengths in trigonometry, particularly when a tangent ratio (like tan A = 4/3) is given, enabling learners to determine other trigonometric ratios.

Fig. 8.10: This image shows a right-angled triangle ACB, with the right angle at C. The hypotenuse AB is 29 units, the side BC is 21 units, and the angle at B (∠ABC) is denoted as θ. Learners should identify the opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse sides relative to angle θ.

Fig. 8.11: This image displays a right-angled triangle ABC, with the right angle at vertex B. Angles A and C are the acute angles of the triangle. Learners should use this general triangle to define and understand trigonometric ratios for angles A or C.

Fig. 8.12: This image shows a right-angled triangle OPQ, with the right angle at vertex P. The side OP is explicitly labeled as 7 cm. Learners should utilize this diagram to apply the Pythagorean theorem and subsequently determine trigonometric ratios for angles O or Q.

Fig. 8.13: This image presents a right-angled triangle PQR, with the right angle at Q. Side PQ measures 12 cm and the hypotenuse PR measures 13 cm. Learners can use these given measurements to find the missing side QR and then compute various trigonometric ratios for angles P and R.

Fig. 8.14: This image depicts a right-angled triangle ABC, with the right angle at B. It shows that angles A and C are both 45 degrees, making it an isosceles right triangle. This visual is instrumental in demonstrating the derivation of trigonometric ratios for a 45-degree angle.

Fig. 8.17: This visual displays a sequence of right-angled triangles where angle A progressively decreases, approaching 0 degrees. Learners should observe how as angle A shrinks, the side BC becomes shorter, and the hypotenuse AC approaches the length of side AB. This demonstrates the limiting behavior of trigonometric ratios for small angles, like sin(A) approaching 0 and cos(A) approaching 1.

Fig. 8.18: This visual presents a series of right-angled triangles illustrating how the triangle changes as angle A increases and approaches 90 degrees. Learners should notice that as angle A increases, point A moves closer to B, side BC becomes longer, and side AC becomes almost equal to BC, while AB approaches zero. This demonstrates the limiting behavior of trigonometric ratios for angles approaching 90 degrees, like sin(A) approaching 1 and cos(A) approaching 0.

Fig. 8.21: This visual displays a right-angled triangle labeled ABC, with the right angle at vertex B. A small arc indicates an acute angle at vertex A. This fundamental geometric shape is used to define trigonometric ratios.

Fig. 9.1: This visual demonstrates the concept of 'Angle of elevation' using a person observing the top of a tall tower. Fig. 9.2: This visual illustrates the 'Angle of elevation' with a person looking up at a distant object in a mountainous landscape. It clearly labels the 'Horizontal level' extending from the observer's eye and the 'Line of sight' to the object, with the 'Angle of elevation' being the angle between these two lines.

Fig. 9.3: This visual explains the 'Angle of depression' with a person on a balcony looking down at an object on the ground. It shows the 'Horizontal level' from the observer's eye and the 'Line of sight' directed to the object, explicitly labeling the 'Angle of depression' between them.

The distance from the observation point C to the base of the tower B (BC) is given as 15 m, and the angle of elevation from C to the top of the tower A (angle ACB) is 60 degrees. The accompanying text box shows the formula tan 60° = AB/BC, illustrating how to calculate the height of the tower.

Fig. 9.7: This image displays a geometric diagram illustrating the measurement of the height of a flagstaff on top of a building. It shows a point P on the ground, a building AB, and a flagstaff DB, forming two right-angled triangles PAB and PAD, with angles of elevation 30° and 45° respectively from point P. The accompanying text includes trigonometric equations relating the height of the building (AB) and the distance from the observer (AP) using `tan 30°`.

Fig. 9.8: This image presents a geometric diagram showing a tower AB and its shadow at two different times of day, creating two right-angled triangles. The text defines BC as the shadow length when the Sun's altitude is 60°.

Fig. 9.9: This image features a geometric diagram illustrating a problem involving two buildings of different heights and the angles of elevation and depression from one to the other. It shows a multi-storeyed building PC and a shorter building AB, depicting a transversal PB cutting parallel lines PQ and BD, hinting at alternate interior angles. The text defines the context for finding the height of the multi-storeyed building and the distance between them.

Fig. 9.10: This diagram illustrates a bridge over a river, showing two right-angled triangles formed by a point P on the bridge (3m high) and points A and B on opposite banks. Fig. 10.1: This visual presents three diagrams illustrating the possible relative positions of a line PQ with respect to a circle: (i) no intersection, (ii) intersection at two distinct points, and (iii) intersection at exactly one point. It helps learners distinguish between a non-intersecting line, a secant, and a tangent.

Fig. 10.2: This diagram illustrates a real-world application of a tangent, showing a rope passing over a pulley. The ropes on either side of the circular pulley act as tangents, touching the circle at a single point. This helps learners relate abstract geometric concepts to practical scenarios.

Fig. 10.3 (i): This visual demonstrates the concept of a tangent as a limiting case of a secant. It shows various lines passing through a fixed point P, intersecting the circle at two points (Q1, Q2, Q3, R1, R2, R3), and then evolving into a line (A'B') that touches the circle at exactly one point, P, as the other intersection point merges with P. This dynamically illustrates how a secant transforms into a tangent.

Fig. 10.4: This image displays a circle, representing a wheel, resting on a flat horizontal line, representing the ground. A small square symbol indicates that the radius drawn to the point of contact between the wheel and the ground forms a right angle with the ground. This visual helps demonstrate the property that the radius at the point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent.

Fig. 10.5: This diagram illustrates a circle with center O, a tangent line XY touching the circle at point P. A point Q is shown on the line XY, and a dashed line segment OQ connects the center to Q, while OP is a solid radius to the point of tangency. The diagram visually supports the idea that the radius OP is the shortest distance from the center O to the line XY, implying perpendicularity.

Fig. 10.7: This diagram shows a circle with center O, an external point P, and two tangent segments PQ and PR drawn from P to the circle. Radii OQ and OR are drawn to the points of tangency, Q and R respectively. This setup is typically used to illustrate and prove that the lengths of tangents from an external point to a circle are equal (PQ = PR).

Fig. 10.10: This diagram illustrates a circle with center O, two tangents TP and TQ drawn from an external point T, and a chord PQ connecting the points of tangency. The line segment OT connects the center to the external point T and intersects the chord PQ at point R. Numerical values for the radius (5 cm), chord length (8 cm for PQ), and a right angle at R are also indicated, setting up a problem for calculating lengths using geometric properties.

Fig. 10.11: This diagram illustrates a circle with center O and two tangents, TP and TQ, drawn from an external point T. Radii OP and OQ are drawn to the points of tangency, forming a quadrilateral OPTQ, and highlights the relationship between the central angle ∠POQ and the angle formed by the tangents ∠PTQ. A learner should notice that OP ⊥ PT and OQ ⊥ QT, forming right angles at P and Q, and that the sum of angles in quadrilateral OPTQ is 360°.

Fig. 10.12: This diagram shows a quadrilateral ABCD that circumscribes a circle, with the points of tangency labeled P, Q, R, and S on sides AB, BC, CD, and DA respectively. It visually represents the property that the sum of the lengths of opposite sides of such a quadrilateral are equal (AB + CD = AD + BC). A learner should notice how the lengths of tangents from each vertex to the circle are used to derive this property.

Fig. 11.2: This diagram displays a circle with center O and a chord AB, which divides the circle into two regions: a minor segment (APB, shaded) and a major segment (AQB, unshaded). It visually defines and differentiates between these two types of segments, which are formed by a chord and an arc of the circle. A learner should notice that the minor segment is smaller than a semicircle, and the major segment is larger.

Fig. 11.3: This diagram illustrates a sector OAPB of a circle with center O and radius 'r', where the central angle is denoted by θ. The shaded region represents the sector, which is bounded by two radii and the arc connecting their endpoints. A learner should observe how the area of a sector is proportional to its central angle and is a fractional part of the entire circle's area.

Fig. 11.4: This visual demonstrates the derivation of the formulas for the area of a sector and the length of an arc using the unitary method, accompanied by a diagram of a circle with a highlighted sector. Learners should observe how the formulas are proportionally derived from the full circle's area and circumference based on the central angle θ.

Fig. 11.5: This visual shows the application of the sector area formula with specific values (angle 30 degrees, radius 4 cm) for a numerical calculation, alongside a diagram of a circular sector. Learners can see the direct substitution of values into the formula and the resulting calculation.

Fig. 11.6: This visual presents a circular sector with a central angle of 120 degrees and a radius of 21 cm. The diagram clearly labels these dimensions, providing the necessary information for a geometric problem involving sector properties.

Fig. 11.7: This visual illustrates an isosceles triangle OAB within a circle, with an altitude OM drawn from the center O to the chord AB, bisecting angle AOB into two 60-degree angles. Learners should notice how this construction creates right-angled triangles, allowing for the application of trigonometric ratios like cosine to find unknown lengths.

Fig. 11.8: This visual features a diagram of a horse tied at the corner of a square field, demonstrating a real-world application of finding the area a tethered animal can graze, which forms a sector of a circle. The surrounding text presents various problems related to calculating areas of sectors and segments in different contexts.

Fig. 11.10: This visual shows an open umbrella from the side and a top-down view of its canopy. The top-down view clearly illustrates the umbrella's canopy divided into 8 equal sectors by its ribs, demonstrating how a real-world object can be modeled as a circle divided into sectors. Learners should notice how the ribs create equal angular divisions, which is crucial for calculating the area of one sector.

Fig. 12.1: This visual displays four fundamental three-dimensional geometric solids: a cuboid, a cone, a cylinder, and a sphere, labeled (i) through (iv). Learners should notice the distinct characteristics and basic shapes of each solid, which are building blocks for understanding more complex composite shapes.

Fig. 12.2: This visual presents a tanker truck designed for carrying liquids, highlighting its tank component. The text describes the tank as being a combination of a cylinder with two hemispheres at its ends. Learners should observe how real-world objects are often composed of simpler geometric solids, making it possible to apply geometric principles to calculate their volumes or surface areas.

Fig. 12.3: This visual displays a test tube, a common laboratory item, and the accompanying text identifies it as a combination of a cylinder and a hemisphere. Learners should recognize that many objects around us are composites of basic geometric shapes, which is a key concept for calculating their surface area and volume.

Fig. 12.4: This visual illustrates a three-step process of combining geometric solids: starting with a cylinder and two separate hemispheres, then showing the hemispheres moving towards the cylinder, and finally depicting them joined to form a single composite solid. This diagram visually explains how complex shapes can be decomposed into or composed from simpler forms, which is essential for understanding how to calculate their combined surface areas or volumes.

Fig. 12.5: This image illustrates the process of combining a cone and a hemisphere to form a toy. It shows how the flat bases of the cone and the hemisphere are joined together to create a smooth, composite solid. A learner should notice that the joined bases disappear from the total surface area calculation.

Fig. 12.7: This diagram illustrates a decorative block composed of a cube with an edge of 5 cm, surmounted by a hemisphere with a diameter of 4.2 cm. It visually represents a composite solid formed by placing a hemisphere on top of a cube. A learner should notice the dimensions provided for both the cube and the hemisphere.

Fig. 12.8: This diagram displays a toy rocket, which is a composite solid made of a cone mounted on a cylinder, along with a cross-sectional view of its base. It shows the total height of the rocket as 26 cm, the conical part's height as 6 cm, the base diameter of the conical portion as 5 cm, and the base diameter of the cylindrical portion as 3 cm. A learner should notice the different radii and heights of the component shapes and how they fit together.

Fig. 12.9: This diagram illustrates a bird-bath, which is a composite solid formed by a cylinder with a hemispherical depression at one end, supported by legs. It provides the height of the cylinder as 1.45 m and its radius as 30 cm. A learner should notice the combination of a cylinder and an inverted hemisphere and the conversion needed between meters and centimeters.

Fig. 12.11: This diagram illustrates an article made from a cylinder, where hemispherical portions have been scooped out from both ends. The blue striped area indicates the visible surface, showing that the inner curved surface of the hemispheres and the outer curved surface of the cylinder contribute to the total surface area. A learner should notice how the removal of material affects the calculation of the total surface area, specifically that the original circular bases of the cylinder are replaced by the curved surfaces of the hemispheres.

Fig. 12.12: This diagram depicts an industrial shed, composed of a cuboidal base topped by a half-cylinder, also known as a semi-cylinder. Dimensions are clearly marked: the cuboid's base is 7m by 15m, and its height is 8m, with the semi-cylinder having a diameter of 7m and a length of 15m. A learner should notice how the overall complex shape is broken down into simpler, recognizable geometric solids for volume calculation.

Fig. 12.13: This diagram illustrates a cylindrical glass with a hemispherical raised portion at its base. The dotted lines indicate the full capacity of a simple cylinder, while the solid lines highlight how the raised hemisphere reduces the effective internal volume of the glass. A learner should notice that the volume of the raised hemispherical part needs to be subtracted from the total volume of the cylinder to find the actual capacity.

Fig. 12.14: This diagram displays a composite toy, formed by a hemisphere surmounted by a right circular cone, perfectly fitted inside a right circular cylinder. The toy shares the same base diameter as the cylinder, and the total height of the toy matches the cylinder's height. A learner should observe that the dimensions of the cylinder are directly determined by the dimensions of the cone and hemisphere within it, which is crucial for calculating the difference in volumes.

Fig. 12.15: This image shows several gulab jamuns, each shaped as a cylinder with hemispherical ends, submerged in sugar syrup within a container. The visual provides a real-world example of a solid formed by combining basic geometric shapes. A learner should recognize that each gulab jamun can be deconstructed into a cylindrical body and two hemispheres for mathematical calculations related to their volume or surface area.

Table 13.1: This image presents 'Example 1' with a problem statement about marks obtained by 30 students and a frequency distribution table (Table 13.1). The table lists 'Marks obtained (x_i)' ranging from 10 to 70 and 'Number of students (f_i)' as their corresponding frequencies. Learners should notice how raw data can be organized into a clear frequency table to summarize information and prepare for statistical calculations like the mean.

Table 13.2: This image displays Table 13.2, which is a frequency distribution table for grouped data, showing 'Class interval' (e.g., 10-25) and the 'Number of students' (frequency) for each interval. The accompanying text explains the concept of a 'class mark' as the mid-point of a class interval and provides the formula for calculating it: (Upper class limit + Lower class limit) / 2. Learners should notice how continuous data is grouped into intervals and how to find the representative value (class mark) for each interval using the provided formula.

Table 13.3: This image presents Table 13.3, an extended frequency distribution table for grouped data, showing 'Class interval', 'Number of students (f_i)', 'Class mark (x_i)', and the product 'f_i x_i'. It includes totals for frequencies (Σf_i = 30) and products (Σf_i x_i = 1860.0), along with the formula for the mean (x̄ = Σf_i x_i / Σf_i) and its calculated value of 62. Learners should notice the systematic calculation steps for finding the mean of grouped data using the Direct Method, and how each column contributes to the final mean calculation.

Table 13.4: This image displays Table 13.4, an extended frequency distribution table used for calculating the mean of grouped data using the Assumed Mean Method. It includes 'Class interval', 'Number of students (f_i)', 'Class mark (x_i)', 'd_i = x_i - 47.5' (deviations from an assumed mean), and 'f_i d_i'. The table shows totals for frequencies (Σf_i = 30) and the product of frequencies and deviations (Σf_i d_i = 435). Learners should notice the additional columns required for the Assumed Mean Method, particularly the calculation of deviations (d_i) from a chosen assumed mean, and how these intermediate values are used.

Table 13.5: This table demonstrates the step-by-step calculation of the mean using the step-deviation method. It clearly shows the class intervals, their corresponding frequencies (f_i), class marks (x_i), deviations from an assumed mean (d_i = x_i - a), step deviations (u_i = (x_i - a) / h), and the product of frequency and step deviation (f_i * u_i). A learner should notice how each column builds upon the previous one to simplify the overall calculation process.

Table 13.7: This table presents a grouped frequency distribution for the percentage of female teachers, alongside intermediate calculations for determining the mean using various methods. It includes class intervals, frequencies (f_i), class marks (x_i), deviations (d_i = x_i - 50), scaled deviations (u_i = (x_i - 50) / 10), and the products f_i*x_i, f_i*d_i, and f_i*u_i. A learner should observe how the assumed mean (a=50) and class size (h=10) are used consistently across the deviation and step-deviation calculations.

Table 13.8: This table shows a frequency distribution of the number of wickets, with varying class sizes, and the number of bowlers for each range. The intervals are 20-60, 60-100, 100-150, and 150-250, with their respective frequencies. A learner should notice that the class intervals are not uniform, which implies that a method like the step-deviation method with a common 'h' value might not be directly applicable without adjustment, or that 'h' will vary.

Table for Exercise 7: This table presents a frequency distribution of SO2 concentration in parts per million (ppm) for 30 localities. It lists six class intervals for SO2 concentration (e.g., 0.00 - 0.04) and their corresponding frequencies. Family size frequency table: This table displays the frequency distribution of family sizes based on a survey of 20 households. It shows class intervals for 'Family size' (e.g., 1-3, 3-5) and the 'Number of families' falling into each interval. A learner should notice that the maximum frequency is 8, which corresponds to the class interval 3-5, indicating it as the modal class.

Table 13.9: This table presents raw frequency data, showing marks obtained by students and the corresponding number of students for each mark. A learner should notice that the marks are not yet ordered, representing the initial collection of data before processing for analysis.

Table 13.11: This table displays marks obtained by students in ascending order along with their cumulative frequencies. A learner should observe how cumulative frequency is calculated by sequentially adding up the number of students for each mark, showing the total number of students up to that particular mark.

Table 13.13: This table provides a complete 'less than' cumulative frequency distribution for marks obtained by students. Class intervals, Frequency, Cumulative frequency: This table displays class intervals, their individual frequencies, and the cumulative frequencies, derived from the data in the previous table.
